subtopic: PINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE- FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
PINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE- FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to present the seventh and final report of the select standing committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government. I am very happy to say this is a unanimous report. It is as follows:
The select standing committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government beg leave to present the following as a seventh and final report:
Your committee to whom was referred for consideration and report the accounts and the estimates of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited, and the various bills presented to parliament relating to the operations of the railways and shipping owned and controlled by the government, held eighteen public meetings, in the course of which they examined many witnesses, including three directors and the necessary executive officers of the company including the president.
1.	Bill No. 21-
5.	our committee had under consideration Bill No. 21 "An Act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to authorize additional provision of moneys to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1931."
The object of this bill was to authorize the Canadian National Railways to issue additional securities to the extent of $11,372,498.86, for the purpose for the year 1931 of financing where the amounts available from net operating income and investments were insufficient.
In other words the Canadian National Railways Financing Act, 1931, which authorized the issue of securities to the principal sum of $68,500,000 the estimated requirements for 1931, was insufficient for the purposes of the railway to the extent above mentioned, and

Railways and Shipping-Report
this bill became necessary by reason of the ascertained income deficit arising from the operations of the railways, and full explanation of this bill was given in the House of Commons by the Minister of Railways and your committee reported the same without amendment.
2.	Bill No. 34-
Your committee also had under consideration Bill No. 34 "An Act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to authorize the provision of moneys to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1932."
The object of this bill was to authorize the Canadian National Railways to issue securities to the extent of $61,500,000 for the purpose during the year 1932 of financing where amounts available from net operating income or investments may be insufficient. This sum is made up of the following:-
(a)	Net income deficits, including profit and loss, but not including interest on Dominion
government advances, not exceeding	$42,784,610
(b)	Equipment principal payments, sinking funds, miscellaneous maturing or matured notes and other obligations secured
or unsecured, not exceeding.. 11,681,651
(c)	Construction and betterments, including coordinations; acquisition of real or personal property, and working capital,
not exceeding	 7,033,738
Total	$61,500,000
The detailed statement of the financial requirements and estimated capital expenditures for the year ending December 31, 1932, was placed before your committee, amounting to the said sum of $61,500,000, and while the management of the system last year expressed their intention of reducing operating expenses and have put into effect economies which they affirm will approximate $28,000,000 in the years 1931 and 1932, yet the difference between estimated operating revenue and estimated operating expenses for the current year falls far short of meeting the interest on the funded debt in the hands of the public, w'hich, without regard to any interest due to the government, this year amounts to the sum of $56,849,244.65, an increase in 12 months of $1,634,267.18. Reference to the annual report of the company shows that the net additional capital expenditure for the period of nine years from January 1, 1923, to December 31, 1931, amounts to the sum of $419,669,620.64 which has imposed an additional annual interest burden of $20,936,821 for the same period and accounts for approximately 37£ per cent in the increase of the annual interest charges due to the public.	There is also
$1,357,650 due the government for interest on unfunded debt.
In the light of the aforegoing it is difficult for your committee to appreciate, from a business standpoint, the wisdom of some of the capital expenditures made and included in the total increase above referred to. Doubtless had the present world depression not so adversely

affected the system or continued for such a great length of time, better results from these capital expenditures would have accrued to the system. In view, therefore, of the results of the past two or three years, your committee strongly recommend that until there is marked improvement in the earnings of the system, capital expenditures should be limited strictly to the barest necessities, always consistent with efficiency.
Your committee had under consideration also the annual report for the year ending December 31, 1931, and have agreed to report the same.
3.	Operating Expenditures-
The operating expenditures for the year 1932, exclusive of eastern lines, are estimated at $139,304,000, while the operating revenues for the same period are estimated at $157,248,000.
The operating revenues for the year 1931 amounted to the sum of $177,273,738, or approximately $20,000,000 more than the estimate for 1932.
In view of the rapid decline of the operating revenues, your committee are impelled to recom-men'd that the most stringent economy be exercised by the management in all the controllable operating expenditures, and in this regard your committee recommend that with respect to executive officers and other salaried officials of the railway, a thorough revision of salaries downward be made. In the report of your committee for the year 1931, a specific recommendation to that effect was passed and in response thereto the report from the subcommittee of the board of directors, directed to the lion, the Minister of Railways and Canals, dated the 16th February, 1932, was submitted to your committee. This report announced that on July 31, 1931, a horizontal cut of ten per cent, affecting all officials and officers in receipt of salaries of $4,000 and over, became effective, and has resulted in an annual saving of $545,652, affecting in all 828 officials and officers. This means that the annual cost of the said 828 officials theretofore amounted to approximately $5,456,200. The sub-commitee of the board of. directors were of opinion that specific rather than further horizontal reductions in salaries should be made, and stated that an examination of the salaries exceeding $5,000 Avas under way, having in view additional economies. No subsequent report lias been received, but your committee concur that specific rather than a further horizontal reduction in salaries should be made, and in this connection desire to point out that in a statement submitted and produced to the committee, it would appear that as of July 21, 1931, there were 96 officials receiving $10,000 and over and 37 officials receiving $15,000 or over. Your committee are of opinion that the salaries paid to the high officials are excessive and should immediately be substantially reduced.
Your committee would further point out that there would seem to be a multiplicity of officials and the number of higher paid officials should be substantially reduced, especially those acting in the capacity of assistants to heads of departments. Your committee therefore recommend that the sub-committee of the board of directors set up to deal with this matter be instructed to put into effect immediately the principles underlying this recommendation.
Included in the activities of the sub-committee of the board dealing with the salaries of the

Railways and Shipping-Report
executive heads and other officials, was the subject matter of the remuneration received by the president. Under the terms of his contract of engagement dated September 23, 1929, the president shall receive a fixed annual salary of $75,000 per annum, without any extra fees or remuneration of any description. It has come to the attention of your committee that the president is still in receipt of an additional $5,000 fee from the Ontario Car Company and the special annual allowance for expenses not to be specifically accounted for approved by the board of directors on November 18, 1929, amounting to $15,000, and your committee recommend that the matter of the receipt of said fee of $5,000 shall be again considered by tbe board of directors with a view to its possible cancellation. With respect to the special allowance of $15,000 your committee recommend that the payment of the same be reviewed by the board of directors as being inconsistent with the terms of his contract of engagement.
Following the recommendation of your committee of last year, made on the suggestion of the president, a Royal Commission on Transportation has been set up by the government and is now functioning. This commission has not yet finished its labours or reported its findings. Your committee are not desirous of anticipating the findings of the commission but your committee are of the opinion that the report of the commission which it is anticipated will be brought down shortly should be studied with the greatest care, not only by the government itself, the systems of railways concerned, but by the Canadian people generally, so that the views of the commission may be thoroughly understood, and if deemed advisable given effect to at the next session of parliament.
4.	Maritime Freight Rates Act and Eastern Lines-
Your committee have also had under consideration item No. 317 in the estimates providing for the payment to the Canadian National Railway Company as required by the Maritime Freight Rates Act of the deficit incurred during the period under review on eastern lines. The amount of the estimated deficit is $6,217,400, and in addition the sum of $1,750,000. representing the estimated amount by which the revenues of the lines will be lessened during the year by the reduction of rates applicable to eastern lines by the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. In view of the legislation existing your committee are of opinion that the amounts asked for are necessary and proper to give effect to the letter and spirit of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and in the operation of the eastern lines. Your committee are, however, of the opinion that the two items above referred to, the deficit in operation of the eastern lines, and the amount required in operation of the eastern lines, and the amount required to reimburse the national railways for reductions in tolls under the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act should not be included in the same estimate. and should be severed and shown separately, even if legislation to effect that end is necessary, and respectfully recommend that appropriate action in the premises be taken so as to provide that the amount required to provide for the payment of the deficit in operation on the eastern lines be entirely severed from the amount required to be paid in reduction of tolls under the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
Your committee has also had under consideration item No. 316, being the amount required under the Maritime Freight Rates Act to provide for payment from time to time during the fiscal year 1932-33 of the difference, estimated by the Board of Railway Commissioners and certified by the said board to the Minister of Railways and Canals, as and when required by him, occuring on account of the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act between the tariff tolls and the normal tolls, referred to in section 9 of the said act, on alt traffic moved during 1932 by the independent railway companies mentioned therein, and your committee are of opinion that this amount is necessary to implement the provisions of the act in that regard and should be granted by parliament.
5.	Canadian Government Merchant Marine-
Your committee have had under consideration
item No. 314 in the estimates, relating to loan to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, to be applied in payment of deficits in operations of the company and of the vessels under the company's control during the year ending December 31, 1932, amounting in all to $440,009, a decrease of $148,500 over the previous year.
Your committee have also considered the balance sheet of the company and are of the opinion that the said sum of $440,000 is required for the purpose of the company and should be granted by parliament. Your committee reiterate their views and believe that the time has come when the government should, if possible, abandon the policy of operating a government merchant marine, and if possible arrange for a sale or lease of the fleet, and where practicable, and not contrary to imperial or inter-dominion relations, make arrangements with other shipping companies so that the trade of Canada may be protected.
6.	Canadian National (West Indies) Service-
Your committee have had under consideration
item No. 315 in the estimates, relating to the loans to the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships. Limited, to be applied in payment of deficits in operations of the company and of the vessels under the company's control, during the year ending December 31, 1932, and interest requirements, which amounts to $820,000 as compared with $755,000 for the year 1931.
The year ending December 31, 1930, resulted in an operating loss of $523,136.98. while the operating loss for 1931 was $446,568.53, which is slightly above the amount of the subsidy previously paid to an independent company by the government for a much inferior service. Your committee are in agreement with the principle that this steamship service is a matter of treaty obligation and should be continued, but your committee are of opinion that the utmost vigilance should be exercised by officials directing and in charge of this steamship line so that, if possible, the cost of operation to the dominion should be reduced to a minimum, consistent with efficiency, and at the earliest possible moment turned into an operating profit. The service performed by this line on both routes is an excellent one and should be constantly brought to the attention of the Canadian people whenever and wherever possible with a view to their patronizing the service.
3134	COMMONS
Railways and Shipping-Report
With respect to the traffic originating in the British West Indies, served by the ships, your committee are of opinion that every effort should be: made to induce the residents and commercial interests in such colonies to patronize the service thus made possible for them at so great an expense by the Canadian people, to the fullest possible extent.
7.	Expense Accounts of Officials-[DOT]
Your committee have had under consideration the question of expense accounts of executive and other officers of the company. After fully considering the matter, your committee desire to record their belief that there should be a much stricter supervision of all expense accounts, and before payment they should be supported by vouchers and that other necessarv evidence of payment should be presented to a properly constituted committee of directors set up for the purpose of examining and passing on same and that payment of all such expense accounts, whether submitted bv the president executive heads or all other officials should be strictly limited to business purposes and that with respect to company entertainment accounts, only those authorized by the same separate «mcl controlling body should be approved. Last year your committee made a strong recommendation in reference to this matter and reiterate what was then said, especially in relation to such matters as club dues, entertainments and donations. A system of control similar to that in vogue in the best regulated industrial houses, finance and other institutions is required, and your committee earnestly recommend that the board of directors forthwith put in effect such effective control as is necessary in the premises. The subject matter is one that cannot be effectively dealt with by a parliamentary committee but the principle involved is an important one, and in the opinion ot your committee the best qualified body to deal with the matter is the board of directors.
These recommendations should apply specifically to all officers of the company irrespective of their rank or station.
8.	Audit-
According to the evidence submitted to your committee on a previous occasion it has b^en shown that the government employs a reputable hrm of chartered accountants to make a running audit of the railway operations. The auditors sign the annual report and give a certificate attached to the consolidated balance sheet in which they state:-
"We have examined the books and records of the companies comprising the Canadian National railway system for the twelve months ended the 31st December, 1931. The investments in road and equipment appearing in the of the companies as at the 1st January, 1J23, were accepted by us.
We certify that, in our opinion, the above consolidated balance sheet is properly drawn up 8° a.s exhibit a true and correct view of the attains of the system as at the 31st December, ailc* we further certify that, in our opinion, the relative income and profit and loss accounts for the year ended the 31st December, 1931, are correctly stated."
^ our committee are of opinion that the audit now in effect is not sufficient and should go much further, and the auditors should be empowered to go into every phase of the system's operations with power to call atten-
tion to any matter calling for comment in their judgment similar in principle to the powers vested in the auditor General of Canada.
9.	Financial Control-
Heretofore there has been control of the capital expenditures of the company but down to a comparatively recent date the expenditures on operation were vested entirely in the executive heads of departments, and were subject only to the review of the president. No such power should be vested in any one man or small group of men under the same control.	In no sense can such a system be
deemed to be effective, and in the opinion of your committee, this position should be remedied forthwith.
On the 2nd June, 1931, a special by-law No. 18 was enacted by the board of directors establishing a finance committee under the authority of the statute relating to the company, which by-law was duly ratified by order in council No. P.C. 1398, passed on the 17th June, 1931. There was already governmental control of capital expenditures under the statute.	By-law No. 18 provides for the
setting up of a committee of the board of directors to be known as a "finance committee" to consist of three members of the board, namely, the president of the company who was to be the chairman of the committee, the director holding the position of deputy minister of railways and canals, and the director holding the position of vice-president in charge of the legal affairs of the company. The by-law further provides that such finance committee shall, notwithstanding anything in any other by-law to the contrary, have supervision and control over all matters relating to the capital expenditures of the company, and particularly in respect to the provision of the moneys therefor and the allocation of such moneys. The by-law as enacted and confirmed is silent with respect to expenditures for operation and maintenance and in the opinion of your committee the scope of the by-law should be immediately enlarged by appropriate action on the part of the board so as to provide that two additional members of the board shall also be members of the finance committee and that all expenditures for materials and/or supplies, or expenditures of any other character, save and except payrolls, amounting in value to say $25,000 or over, should first be passed upon by the finance committee and subsequently ratified by the board or the executive committee. Your committee are of the opinion that such a provision would have a healthful and beneficial effect not only on the volume of purchases, especially as unanimity on the part of the entire committee is necessary under the terms of the by-law, but also the manner and character of purchases, and your committee earnestly recommend that immediate steps be taken by the board to give effect to the principles underlying this recommendation.
10.	The President's Residence-
Your committee had under consideration the fact that on the eighth of August, 1930, pursuant to a resolution of the board of directors passed on September 23. 1929, the residence No. 1415 Pine Avenue, Montreal, was leased by the railway company for a period of ten years, as a residence for the president at an annual cost closely approximating $20,000.

Railways and Shipping-Report
Having regard to all the evidence adduced and having special regard to the president's contract of engagement, dated September 23, 1929, as ratified and confirmed by his contract with the government dated October 25, 1929, whereby the prisident agreed to serve as president and chairman of the company, including the various constituent and subsidiary companies comprising the system, and for the full and entire services to be performed from time to time for the fixed annual salary of $75,000, without any extra fees or remuneration of any description, and in addition, but subject to the by-laws, rules and regulations applicable, all reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred in connection with the duties of his office or offices, your committe are of opinion that the leasing of the residence appears to your committee to be in contravention of the contract of engagement and even if legal was unwise and should not have been authorized.
The whole transaction in the opinion of your committee was a successful attempt by the board of directors to do indirectly what could not be done directly by expenditure on capital account, namely, to procure a residence for the president free of rent, taxes and repairs, and your committee consider that the action of the board of directors in this regard indicates that while they may not have exceeded their legal powers they did not exercise that degree of prudence, care and judgment requisite in the premises.
Your committee recommend that the whole transaction be reviewed and investigated by the directors, with a view to ascertaining its legality, and if possible obtaining its recision.
11.	Off-Line Offices in the United States-
In recent years a large number of off-line passenger and freight offices have been established in leading cities of the United States, with a view to obtaining traffic for both branches of the service.
Data received with respect to the expenses of and gross receipts from all such offices show that results have been fairly satisfactory with respect to freight traffic but with respect to passenger traffic the results achieved so tar liave not been commensurate with the cost.
Your committee investigated with some care the situation with respect to the New York passenger office now located at 673 Fifth Avenue. The initial cost of acquiring these premises and of alterations amounted to the sum of $429,223.05, and the annual cost of operation including the rental of the premises 505 Fifth Avenue, formerly occupied as passenger offices and which are still under lease and at present unoccupied, is now $252,902. The °toss amount of passenger traffic sold in 1931 was $502,353, including transportation sold on other lines.
Your committee recommend that the whole question of the New York and other off-line passenger offices should be carefully reviewed by the management in conjunction with the board of directors.
Your committee further recommend that careful consideration be given by the management and by the board to the question of closing such of the offices, both passenger and freight, as have not achieved satisfactory results, and also of cooperating with other railway systems by joint arrangement so as to effect as much saving as possible.
12.	Pensions-
A memorandum respecting the various pension schemes in effect was submitted to your committee.
On December 31, 1931, there were 2,476 retired officials and employees on the pension list and the total pensions paid for 1931 amounted to 1,248,000.83.
These pension systems comprise: -
(1)	The Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railway employees provident fund, which is still in force.
(2)	The Grand Trunk Railway of Canada superannuation and provident fund, scheme, closed in 1907 and the presently subsisting Grand Trunk scheme.
(3)	The Canadian National Railway pension scheme, set up in 1929, and in force at the present time.
All of the above mentioned schemes have legislative sanction and authority, but inasmuch as in a return filed with your committee it appears that during the past five years numerous employees received pensions in excess of what the pension schemes applicable to such employees call for your committe are of opinion that attention should be called to this apparent excess of jurisdiction.
Your committee are of opinion that the whole situation respecting pensions should be reviewed, not with any view to reducing statutory pensions but with the view to putting the pension schemes on a sound economic basis, including, if deemed desirable, the inclusion of . the principle of contribution.
Your committee is of opinion that inasmuch as the pension schemes now in effect are statutory the payment of amounts in excess of the amounts called for by such schemes are not justified in principle, and your committee recommend that the attention of the board of directors be called to this situation, with a view to taking such action in the premises as may be deemed desirable and just, having regard to the fact that the principle of pensions is an established principle and crystallized into legislation.
13-	.
Your committee realizing that the exercise
of political patronage or influence in the operation of this publicly-owned enterprise would do great injury recommend continued vigilance on the part of all concerned, to avoid the introduction of practices so detrimental to the public interest.
Your committee recommend that the proceedings and evidence taken be printed as an appendix to the Journals of the House, and that 700 copies be printed in blue book form, 500 in English and 200 in French.
Your committee are glad to state that the report is unanimous.
A copy of the minutes of proceedings and evidence is tabled herewith, all of which is respectfully submitted.
R. B. Hanson,
Chairman.
By unanimous consent, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Duff, that the seventh and final report of the select standing

Railways and Shipping-Report
committee on railways owned, operated and controlled by the government, be concurred in.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to make any reference to the past of the railway system. In that past there may be something to forgive and much to forget. In the report itself, I find much that is pious and something that is practical. It is encouraging in that it is unanimous; it shows that an attempt is being made to lift the railways out of party strife, that is eminently commendable. But what is discouraging is that to-day, when the country is faced with such terrible obligations and when such heavy demands are made upon its purse, no suggestion has been made whereby the tremendous losses resulting from the operation of the roads might be further and substantially and immediately curtailed.
What about the royal commission?

It is true that a royal
commission has been appointed, composed of very eminent ma. We have reason to hope that a finding will be made which will enure to the benefit of the people of Canada and help both railway systems. But as I had occasion to say some time ago, this report cannot be made available for some time, and it cannot be made effective until the lapse of further time, I was therefore hoping that out of this understanding which appears to have been arrived at by the members of all parties who formed the committee some practical and unanimous suggestion might come whereby the tremendous expenses of useless competition could at least temporarily be curtailed.
We had it from the president of the national system that the expense of competition was very great indeed, and there was an inference from what he said that tremendous savings could still be made without seriously impairing the effectiveness of the service, if competition and the expense arising from it could be eliminated. I am of those who believe that if this committee could have accentuated that fact, that if a unanimous committee representing all parties in the house had impressed upon all the roads in Canada the absolute necessity, for the time being, of keeping down these expenses, it- would have been productive of results. We have heard on all sides forebodings, ominous statements have been made of the perils which overhang the country today ; yet here is an opportunity of saving, some $50,000,000 to $100,000,000 in the operation of the two railways, in the next twelve

months. The principal obstacles in the way of effecting those economies are the faces that have to be saved.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a unanimous and forceful recommendation from the committee would have had to be heeded both by the government-owned roads and by those privately-owned. We have been told that this drain upon the financial energies of the country is the greatest financial peril that confronts us to-day, and it seems to me regrettable that the committee has not considered the possibility of temporary and immediate economies.
With regard to the merchant marine, the report is about what it was last year. There was a recommendation last year that the service be suspended and that the boats be given away or cease to be operated. They have been operated for another year and the net result is that another half million has been lost. And apparently the same procedure will be followed again this year. I understand that hon. gentlemen of the special committee have agreed not to debate this report. I am not bound by that agreement. I hope, however, that I have said nothing which is controversial in a party sense, which will provoke recriminations from the other side of the house. I firmly believe what I have said, and believing it, I felt it was my duty to speak as I have.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
It seems to me that it is
hardly in order that a report of this character should be submitted to the house and a few minutes later concurrence moved. I take it that a report of as great importance as this ought to lie on the table for a day at least, until members have had on opportunity of reading it. It is not good practice that we should simply pass this report as a matter of form, even though it comes as a unanimous report from the committee. How-.ever, I should like to make a few remarks with reference to what has been said by the last speaker (Mr. Hackett). He suggests that there has been no report on the major problems of transportation in this country. I had thought that we all understood that the committee could not very well discuss these problems while they were under consideration by a royal commission, so that under the circumstances I do not see that the committee could have done anything else than it has done at the present time. But when the hon. member, in closing his address, suggested that he hoped he had not raised any controversial questions, I must enter my protest against his assumption that we all agreed with him.

Railways and Shipping-Report
The hon. member suggests that there are tremendous losses resulting from the operations of the road. By centering attention on the Canadian National Railways he is apt to give the impression that it is because of the public ownership of this road that the losses have occurred. I submit that there are tremendous losses resulting from the operation of the Canadian Pacific Railway at the present time. If anyone will consider the way the shares of the Canadian Pacific have dropped within the last few months, he must be convinced that that road also is in a condition which is far from satisfactory.
It is quite true that the Canadian Pacific Railway does not come under review in this house as the Canadian National does. As someone suggests, it is a pity that it does not, since it has been so largely built up by public funds; and since it has been maintained by the public, seeing that there is no other way of maintaining it, there being often involved the payment of heavy freight rates by the public to say nothing of subsidies. Under these conditions, it does seem to me that its operations might come under review in this house. It is hardly fair at any rate to criticize to the last detail the operations of the Canadian National Railways and let the other road go without criticism.
As I tried to point out last year, when the report of the committee was under consideration, by centering attention on all these details of the Canadian National Railways, the public is led to think that there has been the utmost extravagance. Undoubtedly, there has been extravagance. But I submit that similar extravagance is a commonplace in other corporations. Someone mentions Lucerne. Yes; and a score of things connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway which are extravagances do not come under review in this house, even though the expense must ultimately be borne by the people of Canada.
Do two wrongs make a right?
No, but it is not always wise to center on one wrong to the absolute exclusion of another.
All we had to do was to examine this road.

I am not in the slightest blaming the committee; I am prepared to vote for the report of the committee. I cannot see how the committee can report otherwise. But I do point out that we are examining only one road; indeed I am not for the moment discussing the report of
the committee but rather the statement made by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett).
What statement?
The statement was made that there were tremendous losses resulting from the operation of the road.
All railroads in Canada?
That is all I want to hear-from all railroads in Canada.
That is what I said.

That is not what the speaker said; he said there were tremendous losses resulting from the operations of the road, that is, the Canadian National Railways. In all fairness I want to point out that there are also tremendous losses resulting from the operation of other roads.
That is what I said.

I did not catch that, but as long as it is admitted, that is all I want. The member for Stanstead also referred to the useless competition being carried on and urged that it should be curtailed. He quoted the president of the Canadian National Railways as saying that savings could be made if competition could be eliminated. I have no doubt that that statement is true and I agree with it. I am very glad that we are getting away from the old idea that competition is the life of trade and are beginning to learn that the contrary is true. We are beginning to learn that railway operation is by its very constitution in the nature of a monopoly. I quite agree with what I believe to be the position taken by the hon. member, that sooner or later we will have to have an amalgamation of the roads in this country, but I contend it should be not only an amalgamation of the railroads but an amalgamation of our whole transportation system including railroads, motor service and air service. I think that will have to come sooner or later but when it does come some of us will insist that it will not be a private monopoly but rather a great public service. Like the hon. member for Stanstead I hope I am not saying anything which will prove to be very controversial. If we are all agreed on my proposal, there is not very much more to be said on the matter. However, I think I have as much right to take my statement for granted as has the hon. member. It seems to me that there is a useless waste in all competition and we should not centre on this one particular instance. Competitive industry involves an enormous waste and if I

Railways and Shipping-Report
understand anything of the general trend today in business, not merely in transportation but in all productive industry, there is a tendency to eliminate waste and develop monopoly. I think monopoly is bound to come but when it comes we will insist that it must not be a private monopoly but a government monopoly. I hope that one of these days those principles which were so clearly enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) with regard to air control will be put into practice with regard to transportation control.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is only one observation which I should like to make. I should not like the country to understand that it would be possible by giving effect to any recommendation of the committee to make a saving of $50,000,000 in twelve months. It is perfectly ridiculous .to make any such statement because that cannot be done under present conditions in this country. We must realize this when we consider the sum total of the revenues of all Canadian railroads and appreciate that the railway situation on this continent is one which beggars all description. The shares of the New York Central Railroad are to-day selling for less than $12 whereas a few months ago they were selling at over $200 each. Practically the same condition exists in connection with the shares of the Pennsylvania Railroad. The Baltimore and Ohio Railway has passed its preferred dividends and the shares of all trunk line systems in the United States have fallen to a market price that one could never have possibly anticipated. The Postmaster General will realize the exact situation if he considers that these people find it impossible to get their mail more than once or twice a week. If the hon. Postmaster could accede to my request, these settlers would regularly receive their mail.

I strongly support the request of this association. As a doctor, I must, first, inform you that these civil servants live in an atmosphere and conditions quite exceptional. They do not live a regular life, are continuously exposed to danger, breathe coal fumes during their whole life time, and have to put up with continuous vibrations during their working hours. I have no statistics on the subject at my disposal, however, I am convinced beforehand that, if such statistics could be collected, they would show that the average length of life for these employees is much shorter than among the ordinary workmen. I therefore beg of the Postmaster General to take this request under his serious consideration.

Postmaster General stated publicly, on more than one occasion, that he would protect even against his friends, the postmasters who had fulfilled their duties and the employees of his department who had taken no active part in politics. Was it to compromise that the hon. Mr. Chairman, I think the

Yesterday I had two desks filled with my files and to-day, in order to expedite business, I have reduced the number of documents to what I hold in my hand.
I am ready to proceed and to show my goodwill, but if there is objection, the debate on the Post Office estimates will last for a week. I am being fair to all, but I wish to be treated fairly. I have points to make and part of the work of the session is to point out what has been done. I complain very much of the fact that especially in Quebec the sour-mouthed defeated candidates, are worse offenders in respect of dismissals than the Conservative members. This is the point I wish to make to the committee and the country. When there are so many unemployed, so many who are suffering and in dire distress, we see these defeated candidates and members wasting the time of the Postmaster General by asking him to cut off the heads of numerous people who, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Montmagny has said, are innocent of political partisanship and yet are treated in the same way as if they had paraded the streets and made speeches in favour of Liberal candidates. Probably not, Mr. Chairman, but what I am after is justice and fairness. When investigations are carried on fairly, and when fair play is exercised, I have no objection. When after investigation the

commissioners state that there is nothing against a man, but make a report against him I say they deal most unfairly, and it is against that sort of practice I complain.
I have said nothing about requests for investigations made by Conservative members of this house. I care noit whether they come from the province of Quebec or any other province. I did not complain about them, but I do complain about the fact that the defeated Tory candidates in the province of Quebec are always asking for the heads of postmasters, so that they may replace them with people who are often not worthy of the positions, and have not the qualifications of their predecessors. I have written the Postmaster General telling him that so far as I am concerned I have no Objection. If he wishes he may dismiss all the postmasters in my constituency, because by so doing he would be helping me politically. I do not object to his cutting off heads; from a political standpoint. I do not object to that.
But I would object.

I congratulate the minister on his response, and I hope he will realize that hon. members on this side are better friends of his than the people who advise dismissals. I should like to make a statement which will make matters somewhat clearer to hon. members, and particularly the hon. member for Montmagny. The young members of this house who have not the experience which they will acquire if they pass thirty-five years here, will learn later on that it is dangerous pastime to go about changing postmasters and trying to please everybody. Hear! Hear!

By an extraordinary coincidence-I do not want to hurt anybody-practically in all cases where the department made a temporary appointment, the post office inspector gave a rating that corresponded to that made by the department in the first instance. It is probably a coincidence, but the department's appointments were ratified by the post office inspector.
The Civil Service Commission in the creation of which I had a hand, in this parliament, since I voted in favour of this system in 1908, was required at the outset to deal only with the inside service. Later on, in 1917, we placed the outside sendee under the Act notwithstanding protests on the part of people with considerable experience who believed such a move was a mistake. I note with pleasure to-day that the present administration is beginning to realize the mistake committed at that time. Postmasters whose revenue is less than S3,000 have just been placed under the
control of the department. This is as it always should have been, because in the outside service, the rural postmaster is not a "civil servant" as defined in the act. He is some merchant, blacksmith, or grocer who employs a young girl to attend to the office, who is appointed by the party to which he belongs and who will probably be dismissed when the other party wins. That is the present system. I am pleased to note a change is being made and that henceforth the department itself will make appointments. This will do away with the camouflage that has existed for years under the present system. Appointment of postmasters in the outside service by the Civil Service Commission was a joke. The inspectors told me all in turn that they were absolutely powerless in such cases, they had no officials to investigate conditions that existed in such and such a part of the country, to make the candidates try qualifying examinations, and in last analysis they were compelled to go by the post office inspector's report. This inspector is an employee of the Pest Office department. He acts for the Civil Service Commission, but he is nevertheless an employee of the department and a man who is naturally pretty well acquainted with the sentiments prevailing in the district, who knows the intentions of the defeated candidate or the member who represents the riding. When he goes to a post office to conduct an investigation, whether it is a matter of coincidence or otherwise, this "rating" is always in favour of the man selected by the administration of the day. That is the old system. I am pleased to note that proceedings will henceforth be conducted openly and that the system applied years ago will be revived.
When I had the honour of being elected a member for the first time, there were no such things as commissions, no Civil Service Commission, no Railway Commission, no Board of Pension Commissioners, no commission of any kind. The member was the people's real representative. If there was something to 'be done in his riding, he would go and see the minister. The latter trusting him took action in line with his recommendation. The matter was settled and if the member had committed a blunder he was the first to suffer. The electors knew whom to blame, they knew where to place responsibility. To-day, parliament has given up all its powers. We are here merely as voting machines to vote hundreds of millions, even thou-

I am sorry to say I noted in many cases in my county the proceedings were not conducted in that manner. That state of things has the effect of bringing discredit upon the department.
Instructions to that effect are given.

The instructions are not carried out. As a rule the commissioner proceeds to the postmaster's place of business and calls up the other interested parties over the telephone. The investigation starts, the witnesses do not appear. The residents are not surprised at what takes place. They expected as much, they know that all governments dispense their favours to friends.
Conducting proceedings in the open is all to the good. In all the investigations in my county, only two postmasters were held guiltless of the charges levelled against them, and probably by chance, they were two Conservatives. All the others were Liberals. I would certainly not want to be judged on the strength of evidence such as that given when these investigations were held. In a word, that is the state of affairs. The people must have something to do; they must busy themselves with public affairs and have their say. I have a word of advice to give the members: Do not make too many changes in the post offices, you will be all the happier later on.

In view of this and the expressions of opinion given to the inspectors by other business men of the village, I do not feel that the charges made in the affidavits returned herewith warrant a recommendation for any change in postmastership.
That is signed by J. H. Hunter, district superintendent at Saskatoon. Apparently that report should dispose of any complaints made by patrons, but nevertheless after the report had been sent to Mr. Wilson at Humboldt he again insisted that an investigation be made. On June 17, 1931, the department referred this matter to Commissioner George Wilson, who is a barrister at Kinistino, and a brother of E. S. Wilson, the defeated Conservative candidate. After this was done Mr. Symons, the postmaster, sent the Postmaster General the folowing telegram, dated July 28, 1931:
A charge of partisanship against me as postmaster is up for investigation before George Wilson, commissioner, at Jansen, Saskatchewan, Thursday. July thirtieth, two p.m. E. S. Wilson who is a witness was twice Conservative candidate federal election, is a brother of the commissioner holding investigation. I request

some other commissioner be provided to hold investigation as to charges against me to overcome bias in the matter. Kindly give consideration to this subject.
When I heard of this I interviewed the Postmaster General, explaining the matter to him, and he agreed that it was not in the best interests of the public service, and not the best way to determine political partisanship, to have a brother of the defeated Conservative candidate act as commissioner. The hon. gentleman agreed that he would find another commissioner, and I was perfectly satisfied. I felt that if another commissioner were appointed, proper evidence would be brought out and if the postmaster had been guilty of political partisanship he would suffer the consequences. However, as a result of that telegram and the interview I had with the Postmaster General, on July 30 the Deputy Postmaster General wired Mr. George Wilson as follows:
Please suspend all action on investigation re E. J. Symons, postmaster at Jansen. Wire reply.
Of course the commissioner accepted the instructions contained in that telegram and wired that he had cancelled the investigation. Following this, a letter was sent by E. S. Wilson, to the Postmaster General under date of July 31, part of which reads as follows:
My purpose in writing you now is to ask that another commissioner be instructed to proceed with the investigation. It seems unfortunate that instead of my friends at Jansen receiving the cooperation of your department, by I presume press of business or some other substantial reason, everything seems to have been done to delay the procedure. . . .
I would ask that when you instruct another commissioner you have him take up with me personally the matter of a suitable date in order that I may arrange a time with Mr. Bates and with the complainants at Jansen.
The defeated Conservative candidate, then, accepted the decision of the Postmaster General to get another commissioner to conduct this investigation. Now I should like to read the reply of the Postmaster General to this letter. It is under date of August 7, and reads as follows:
I was very pleased indeed to get the full explanation in regard to the investigation in connection with the political charges against the postmaster at Jansen, as I could not quite understand the telegram which we received from the postmaster asking that some other commissioner be called upon to hold the investigation.
Here may I interject that the Postmaster General must have understood it, because I

That letter is dated September 1, 1931. Naturally I was pleased to have the promise of the Postmaster General that he would give personal attention to the evidence in this case when it was received, and under date of September 5 I wrote him as follows:
My protest against the brother of the -defeated candidate acting as commissioner to 41761-199
investigate charges of political partisanship in which his brother was personally interested, was not intended to be personal in any way, as I have not the pleasure of knowing the commissioner in this case, but as a general protest against this kind of thing being done. The investigation was held, and the commissioner sent in the folowing report:
After hearing the witnesses I find:
1. That the postmaster attempted, during the 1926 dominion election campaign, in conversation with the Conservative candidate for the Humboldt constituency, in which Jansen is situate, to discourage the candidate. Further in the same election the postmaster introduced the Liberal candidate for the Humboldt constituency to an elector whereupon the Liberal candidate made remarks to the elector in support of his party. These remarks were made in the presence of the postmaster.
The effect of that is that the postmaster made certain remarks to the Conservative candidate during the time of an election, which remarks were intended to discredit him in his campaign. Whether that can be classed as a charge of political partisanship I do not know. The candidate admitted that he was alone with the postmaster of Jansen at the time, but in his evidence the postmaster said he had no recollection whatsoever of having made remarks of that kind to the candidate. As to the statement that the postmaster introduced me to one of the citizens of the village, I recall that very well. He did introduce me to one of the citizens who was one of the staunchest Conservatives, but that introduction came quite casually. I was standing talking to the postmaster, not talking politics at all, and was introduced to this man, and I did make a few remarks in a jocular way concerning the election. I knew very well that he was a strong Conservative.
The second finding of the commissioner reads:
That the postmaster permitted the use of his automobile for the conveyance of voters to the polls on the day of the provincial election in 1929. Evidence was adduced by the defence to the effect that the car was so used without the knowledge of the postmaster. This evidence I discount.
The facts of the matter in connection with the use of that car are these. The postmaster, according to the evidence adduced, and which was corroborated by other witnesses, was in the hospital at Saskatoon at the time of the provincial election of 1929. He had been in the hospital two weeks prior to the election and remained there two weeks after the election, and I would suggest that a man in hospital is not very fussy about what use

Canadian Postmasters' Association, dated Este-van, Saskatchewan, November 27, 1931. It reads:
Hon. Arthur Sauve,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Ont.
Canadian Postmasters' Association protest strongly against dismissal of Postmaster Ernest Symons of Jansen, Saskatchewan. In view of no evidence of partisanship having been given against him at inquiry and also in view of the fact that the commissioner who conducted the inquiry was the brother of the complainant, public feeling locally is very strong against his dismissal, and our association respectfully asks you that his case be reconsidered in accordance with your promise of August 13, 1930, in which you advised us as follows "I am not infallible but if I should commit an error I shall do my best to repair it."
Briefly, that is the history of the dismissal of the postmaster at Jansen on a charge of political partisanship. Now, I know personally that during the last election in 1930, at any rate, Mr. Symons took no part in the campaign. We have the petition of 358 residents of the district, asking that he be retained; we have the telegrams from the postmasters' association, asking that he be retained; we have the opinion of these postmasters that there was no ground for the conclusion that this man was guilty of partisanship. I have quoted from the telegram from the secretary of the postmasters' association some words of the Postmaster General to the effect that he was not infallible and that if he made mistakes which were brought to his attention he would reconsider them and try to have them rectified. I have also read the statement that the Postmaster General made in Montreal, to the effect that no civil servant need fear anything from any government so long as he did his work. I submit that the record in this case does not bear out the sentiment expressed by the Postmaster 'General at these different times. After the evidence had been submitted to him on several occasions, I went and interviewed him, praying that he reconsider all the evidence in connection with the 'Case. I got a number of promises, but apparently nothing was done, and I submit that if this is the sort of investigation that is going to be carried out when charges of political partisanship are made against postmasters, there might just as well be patronage plain and simple instead of having it camouflaged in this way.
I have not much more to add except that I hope the minister will take a different attitude in the future. I do not expect that there will be any review of this case now, inasmuch as the new postmaster has been appointed, but

Supply-Post Office
I do hope that the minister will review the ease for his own guidance in future. If he will consult the record for the Humboldt constituency since I have had the honour of representing it in this house, he will find that no postmaster has even been dismissed on any charges whatever on my recommendation-never on any charge of political partisanship-and I hope he will keep the record of that constituency clear in the future.

In answer to the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke), all I can say is that my remarks in Montreal explained my feeling at that time and at the present time. I am sorry if a misunderstanding has arisen in the case mentioned by my hon. friend, and I shall be very glad to go further into the matter.

Could the Minister
advise me as to the name of the present-postmaster at Rockglen in the constituency of Willow Bunch? This office was vacated some time ago because of a charge of political partisanship brought against the postmaster, Mr. Sproule. I entered a protest against this dismissal. I might say that this man was appointed some years ago on my recommendation. I went to the village when this matter was -being taken up. Five or six applicants for the position had presented themselves to the people gathered together in the town hall, and they voted to have Mr. Sproule appointed postmaster. This man is a returned soldier and is a member of a Conservative family; none of the family have ever been known to vote Liberal. They come from the old family of Sproules here in the east, and probably some hon. members know what they are like-they are dyed in the wool Conservatives. A year or two ago a feud was started between this man and another man in the district, the other taking a solemn declaration that he was going to get this postmaster some time or other. When the government changed he seized the opportunity to lodge a complaint of political partisanship. I do not know that I should interfere in this matter from a political standpoint, because I think the action taken by the department has gained me many votes in the district. The father and mother of this man are very indignant over the dismissal. The chief complaint against him was that he had been a Liberal scrutineer in a provincial by-election in 1929. Both the scrutineer and the deputy returning officer took their oath that that was not so. Another charge was that he was acting as a Liberal 41761-199J
secretary, but the Liberal secretary has taken his oath that he was not. The facts are that this man is a real estate agent and the returning officer asked him to come up to show him how to open the office to start the poll. He said he would; he was there for ten or fifteen minutes in the morning, and because of that he lost his job. He was doing no scrutineering at all. The board of trade of the village has entered a protest and half a dozen affidavits have been signed by different people in the district protesting against this man being dismissed. The affidavits state that nothing was known of any political activity. A petition was sent in, I think, signed by all but two of the people who patronize this post office protesting against the dismissal. Strange to say, the man who was foremost in having this man dismissed, a returned soldier who had been living with Mr. Sproule some two years ago and who was looking forward to getting the position, did not get the position which he was promised. The department went outside the village some thirty or forty miles and brought in another man to act as postmaster. This man is one of the applicants for the position, but I do not know whether he has been appointed as the permanent postmaster.
Does the hon. gentleman connect my name with that case?
I cannot help it if the hon. member happens to have the same name.

I have not the name of the
present postmaster, but I shall obtain it and let my hon. friend know.

The man who has
applied for the job and who was appointed temporary postmaster is Mr. Lawrence. He is a returned soldier, a blacksmith, who had been living some forty miles out from the village. Apparently there was no one in the district good enough for the position and they went outside. Perhaps the department could not find a Tory in the district. I know this man has put in an application and I was wanting to find out if it had been accepted. As I say, I protest against the dismissal of Sproule because he was a good postmaster even if he was a Conservative. His work was very satisfactory to the patrons of the office. He was not appointed because he happened to be a Conservative, he was appointed because it was thought he would give good service, and I think the department has made a mistake in his dismissal.

Mr. Chairman, for
the last hour I have been debating with myself whether or not to take part in the discussion on these estimates. I am adverse to taking part in a pyrotechnical and polemical discussion on estimates of this kind, but inasmuch as there are two matters in which I am much interested and about which I am very deeply concerned, and inasmuch as many people in my district are agitated over these matters, I think it worth while- to discuss them before the committee. I am very sorry that I was unable to follow fully the hon. members for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) who spoke in French, but I believe the hon. member for Bonaven-ture mentioned the new report and referred to the administration of the Civil Service Commission. I understand the hon. member for Temiscouata referred to men having sore mouths, and while I should like to speak with the sweet tempered moderation of which the poets make so much mention, in view of the extreme nature of these cases I cannot see my way clear to speak in any other tone than that of vigorous protest. I do not know why, but there has been no branch of the administration with which I have had so much trouble as with the Post Office Department, Ever since I came to the house in 1926, the Post Office Department has been a sort of jinx to me, and not only that, but in some respects a destroyer of the ideals which I had brought to the house. I entered parliament as a young man after the election of 1926 and one of the first things that was brought to my attention was the post office case at Mundare. A young high school graduate, George Woitkiw, asked me to intercede on his behalf with the Civil Service Commission. I therefore sent in my recommendation to the secretary of that body; I also visited the- office of the Civil Sendee Commission and made a personal investigation of the case. What did I discover? I discovered, first, that Mr. Woitkiw received by far the largest petition in his favour, namely, 354 as against 115 for Mr. W. A. Stewart; second, he was favoured on pure merit by Doctor Roche, chairman of the commission; third, he received the following favourable recommendation from the district superintendent of postal service:
George Woitkiw has actually been in charge of the work of the Mundare office for the past five years. He is particularly well equipped by reason of education and languages to take care of that office. His disposition and attitude towards the public are all that can be desired. The petition in his favour is to be considered practically the voice of the district, both the English-speaking and other sections, i Mi-. Donnelly.]
Finally, he received the following commendation by the chief examiner, Mr. Bland:
On the three counts of being assistant postmaster, having had six years' experience in the office, and knowing the foreign languages which are necessary for the proper qualifications of the duties, I think Mr. George Woitkiw is the logical choice.
All hon. members will agree with me that, strictly on merit, Mr. George Woitkiw, whom I have just mentioned, should have been given the position of postmaster in the village of Mundare.

Did the returned soldiei
question enter into the matter?

No; not a single
returned soldier applied for the position. George Woitkiw did not get the job. Why? Beoause there- was a nigger in the woodpile, and possibly many -hon. members are interested in knowing who this nigger was. There was a villain who entered into the drama which arose out of my efforts to secure justice for Mr. Woitkiw, as well as to prevent the prostitution of the Civil Service Commission into a mere political patronage dispensary. That nigger in the woodpile was the exPostmaster General. As I have already said, I entered the House of Commons a young man, brimful of all the noble aspirations about which we hear so much, extremely zealous for the public welfare with an overwhelming ambition to reform and set things right, fairly saturated and oozing with evangelistic fervour; in a word, I came here as a young man with the highest of ideals. All those ideals were exploded by this single action of the Post Office Department away back in 1926.
The other day I placed on record Mr. Coolican's letter to the Civil Service Commission, asking, yes, I will say demanding, that the other applicant, that is, Mr. Stewart, friend of the defeated candidate, be given the Mundare postmastership. I do not know who this Mr. Coolican is. He evidently must have been acting under instructions from his department. To make a long story short, in this case I think merit was, figuratively speaking, given a slap in the face and patronage was restored again to its former unholy place. I am sorry to have to mention this matter. The other day a report was brought down in the house in regard to the reformation of the civil service administration, and the question I am asking myself now is: Will this new report and the subsequent legislation implementing its findings be successful in sustaining the merit system, or will they continue to allow the percolation of patronage

Supply-Post Office
into the administration of the Civil Service Commission. On that occasion I expressed the opinion that unless a sufficient check were exercised on that body, and particularly on the Post Office Department and its officials, it would not be long before patronage would again begin to creep into the administration of the commission. I repeat: Unless this check is found and made sufficiently effective, nothing less than a trio of saints of the nature and character of St. Peter, St. John and St. Paul, would ever be able to keep the demon of patronage out of the Civil Service Commission, especially if the new commissioners were after the pattern of that saint of two thousand years ago who cut the ear off a patronage hunter of that time. I would not be so cruel as to suggest that the ex-Postmaster General should have an ear cut off, but if patronage is not eradicated, something of this nature might not after all be a bad idea. In such an event I know a lot of men who would be bereft not only of ears but of arms and legs as well.
My original intention, however, was to discuss, not the Mundare post office, but another matter that comes under the purview of the present administration. On March 23, 1931, I was advised by the district superintendent of postal service that unless fifty per cent of the eligible residents along the newly proposed Ryley route subscribed for rural mail delivery boxes, in other words, unless thirty-two of the sixty-three eligible residents along that route paid for boxes, said rural route would not be placed in operation. The establishment of that route was authorized and the contracts thereon duly awarded in 1930, but I have been told that in consequence of the failure of the residents of the locality to purchase rural mail delivery boxes, the service would not be put into effect. Several weeks ago I interviewed the Postmaster General and his deputy, Mr. Gaboury, and I was informed that the reason the aforementioned rural route was not put into operation was that the number of boxes was too small and the number of subscribers did not come up to the required amount. About twelve days after I had interviewed the Postmaster General, I received the following letter from the office of the district superintendent of postal service:
Edmonton, Alberta,
March 21, 1932.
Re: Ryley No. 2 R.R. proposed Dear Mr. Luchkovich,

In answer to your letter of the 16th instant, regarding the number of boxes on the above, I beg to say that I am taking the matter up personally with the postmaster at Ryley, in an endeavour to increase the number to the required amount.
Should I be successful I will let you know.
Some weeks later I received the following answer from Ryley:
The postmaster at Ryley was asked by the inspector, Mr. Hale of Edmonton, to see that the required number of applicants was raised as_ requested. This has been completed and were sent to Edmonton about three weeks ago. Will you kindly give this your attention.
M. B. West,
Ryley, Alberta.
Now I ask the Postmaster General in all sincerity if he thinks it is fair and just, under the circumstances, to ask these people to raise the number of boxes to the required amount, and then after the Ryley applicants had brought the number up to that amount absolutely refuse to put the rural route into operation. This is downright duplicity, evasion and equivocation.

I would
have liked to say how well things went on. I have but one question to ask the hon. Postmaster General and if he answers favourably, I shall not be obliged to go over the whole pile. I wrote to him, on May 17, in connection with the post office of St. Arsene, and I simply want to know whether I can expect an answer to my letter..
I did not quite catch what the hon. member said.

I wrote to
the hon. Postmaster General on May 17, last, in connection with the post office of St. Arsene. I trust that the Minister has found time to read my letter; I would be much obliged if he could give me an immediate answer.
The hon. member for Temiscouata may rest assured that he will receive an answer to his letter, tomorrow morning.
What will be the answer?

As soon as I
have prepared the answer, I shall forward it to the hon. member.

The Postmaster's answer is very vague, he must understand what I mean, and his answer should be ready.
So that the whole committee may understand my remarks, I shall continue in Eng-
Supply-Post Office

lish. The site of the post office was changed at the request of the son-in-law of the man who is secretary-treasurer. He has said he was inspired by public interest, but he had only the interests of his family at heart. The fact is, however, that the post office was changed at a time when the Postmaster General had no complaint against the postmaster in question. In fact that particular postmaster was supported by several Conservatives in the parish who sent petitions to the minister stating that the man in question had not indulged in party politics, that he had been very quiet and did not bother about politics at all. This particular case is unique in that, although a Liberal, the postmaster was supported by Conservatives.
Not only that, but the minister himself wrote me stating that the management of the post office was satisfactory. Those two points ought to have been sufficient to leave the man in peace. Without any notice being given to the postmaster, however, the office was changed; it was transferred to some other place. At that time I wrote the Postmaster General, and no doubt he regretted what had been done as he regretted what happened at Notre Dame du Lac. He wrote to me that he had no objection to the man making his application to the Civil Service Commission, provided he .offered a new site. That application was made, because the man believed in the minister's word. He was reluctant to apply. After I showed him the minister's letter he asked me, "What kind of man is the minister?" I said, "He is a good man; he is an honest man; you can rely upon him. If he tells you you may file your application you may be sure he will not object to your appointment. You are running the risk, but you are dealing with a fair man." He said, "If the minister is a fair man I will make my application, and if I am not appointed by the Civil Service Commission I shall not complain. If I am appointed by the Civil Service Commission the minister will confirm the appointment, and I shall be perfectly satisfied. I run only a fifty per cent risk." That man was appointed by the Civil Service Commission, but despite the fact the site he has offered is satisfactory, the minister has not yet approved the appointment. Surely the minister does not wish that man to have a wrong opinion of him.
He will not prevent the appointment.

I know that; I see that in his face; I know he will be true to his word. I know he will not disappoint that man who has played the game. He sent his application
fMr. Pouliot.]
in the belief that the minister would stick to his word. I see him saying "yes." Does he mean "yes?" I am through with my speech if he answers "yes."
Is the hon. member carrying on an auction sale?
I hope the minister will fulfil my expectation. Does he mean "yes?"
How much am I offered?
I expect "yes" from the good minister.
