I expect "yes" from his tongue and lips.
I shall do my best.
I shall be disappointed if the minister does not live up to my expectations.

Mr. Chairman, I was requested to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to an act of injustice which, incidentally, did not take place in my constituency, but in the adjacent county, that of Dorchester. Mr. Couture, former postmaster of Frampton, has written to me enclosing the famous statement of the hon. Postmaster General at Montreal, in which it is stated that he extends his protection to postmasters and undertakes to shield them against all ills, annoyances and misfortunes which might happen to them, in a word, he becomes the father and protector of the unfortunate postmasters. Mr. Couture begs of me to inquire from the minister why he has not persevered in his good intentions. Mr. Couture was not dismissed as postmaster because he had taken an active part in politics or because he was guilty of political partisanship-no blame could be attached to him in this connection. Notwithstanding all the efforts of those seeking positions given by the Conservative party in the parish, they could find absolutely nothing against Mr. Couture to justify a dismissal founded on political partisanship. They then had recourse to other means, the site of the post office was changed. Mr. Couture contends that he was never notified of the decision to change the site of the post office, and that he was never given the option of choosing another location for the post office. However, the district superintendent contends that on two different occasions he wrote to Mr. Couture to notify him as follows:
I am instructed by the Postmaster General, through the Post Office Department to request you to kindly find a more convenient locality for the post office.

Supply-Post Office
Mr. Couture, in a sworn statement-and his assistant also makes a sworn statement in that sense-that -never did the letters of Mr. Green, superintendent of the Quebec postal district reach the post office of Framipton. Mr. Couture was never notified that the intention was to change the site of the post office and he was never notified to look for another locality. Finally he was dismissed, and the reason given was that he did not comply with the instructions from Mr. Green, which he swore never having received, a statement which is corroborated by his assistant. If it is a fact that Mr. Green really requested Mr. Couture to look for another locality for the post office, he was more fortunate -than the ipeople of my constituency, to whom the same mishap occurred. At St. Lazare, the postmistress was dismissed when the site of the post office was changed; there was no question of having written to her, or having given her the option of getting another locality. They had nothing to reproach her politically; however, in order to replace her by a Conservative election campaigner they simply changed the site of the post office. Following the provincial election, the new postmaster, at St. Lazare, a man named Belanger, was appointed for services rendered to his party, having held a committee room in his residence-a Conservative committee, needless to say. I wrote to the hon. Postmaster General to request him to dismiss Belanger, since he had dismissed liberal postmasters who were far from being as guilty as Belanger. The Postmaster General, however, answered me very singularly, saying, "He kept a committee room in his home, but that has no importance whatsoever, as he is not yet permanently appointed as postmaster." He was shortly after. He was qualifying to become permanent postmaster.
Mr. Chairman, I avail myself of this opportunity to point out to the Postmaster General a number of other cases; I shall close my remarks in two -minutes.
First, with reference to investigations held, some one suggested to the Postmaster General that he should simplify the procedure. I would suggest to him a more radical reform, namely: to entirely dispense with Such investigations; it would be more honest. These investigations are but a camouflage, it is simply a smoke screen ito mask the intentions of the Postmaster General. Before the inquiry ever begins, the postmaster is, usually, already dismissed or-it is a foregone conclusion-the site is -changed, the -camouflage is but a smoke screen. Why not be honest about it, why not entirely eliminate these investigations? Let the Postmaster General
take the responsibility of the dismissal or of maintaining in office the postmaster.
As evidence that these investigations are a joke, most of the six or seven inquiries held in my constituency were presided over by a former defeated candidate in the county of Bellechasse. Following an inquiry held at La-Durantaye, one of my uncles was dismissed. I think, if the Postmaster General had wanted to display some courtesy towards me, he would have maintained him in office, especially as there was nothing against him. That investigation was presided over by a defeated candidate in the county, and the candidate whom I defeated in 1930 was also entrusted with preparing the evidence and the false witnesses. You will, sir, readily understand what importance can be attached to such inquiries! Instead of holding investigations of that kind, why not act honestly and simply dismiss the unfortunate victim unjustly charged. Moreover, he expects to be dismissed, it is a foregone conclusion: To. the victor belong the spoils!
I now come to the case of Mr. Laurent Tanguay, an employee in the Department of Justice, to whom I often referred. I requested his dismissal. I charged him here, in the house, under my responsibility as a member, with political partisanship. As a member of parliament, I requested an investigation, it was not granted. I charged Tanguay with having openly and impudently taken an active part in politics, during fifteen days. At the last provincial election, he was the principal speaker of the Conservative candidate, in the county of Bellechasse. I thought, as a simpleton: Since postmasters were dismissed for the acts of their children or wife, they would also dismiss Tanguay. I thought that if I lodged a complaint, as member of Parliament, the department would act, an investigation would be held and Tanguay dismissed. I have never heard any further about my complaint and so far, nothing has been done. I was, recently informed, by the reply made by the Postmaster General to the hon. member for Megantic, that Tanguay had thrown off all restrain. The latter, it seems, is an employee in the Justice department but in truth, his duties consist in filling vacancies, he looks after the petty work of "patronage" for the Conservative party, at Quebec. Not only was he given an office in the post office in Quebec-a government building-but he is given an assistant from the Post Office department to help him in his work; his correspondence is forwarded under the privilege of the postal frank of the Quebec District Superintendent.

Mr. Chairman, I never before heard of such a notorious abuse. When the Liberals were in power, those who handled patronage for the Liberal party did not have the impudence of installing themselves in government buildings and making use of the officials for their own work. They did not have the impudence of using the frank for their correspondence. Those are the facts I wanted to point out and against I protest.
Mr. Chairman, I merely want to ask the hon. Postmaster General whether a rural mail service has been established at Riviere-Ouelle, and who has been appointed mail carrier?
The hon. member for Iiamouraska will admit it is somewhat difficult to answer on the spur of the moment. I could give him an answer tomorrow by letter, but I cannot answer him now.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the hon. Postmaster General, when he forwards me that reply, to explain also an anomaly that exists with respect to that appointment. In the first place, on December 10, tenders were called for in connection with this contract. The tenders were opened:	Pierre Boucher, of Riviere-Ouelle,
$510; Louis-Philippe Boucher, $550 and, among others, Alfred Lebel, $594. The day the tenders were received, Alfred Lebel wrote the hon. Postmaster General as follows: Honourable minister:
It was due to an error that I put in a tender of $594 in connection with the Riviere-Ouelle mail contract, rural route No. 1. Please correct my tender and insert the amount of $505 which I am willing to accept.
I	find it somewhat strange that Lebel should have written the day the tenders were to be published, that is December 10, that he agreed to reduce his tender price to $505, exactly $5 lower than that of Pierre Boucher to whom the contract was awarded, nevertheless. Several requests were forwarded to the hon. minister. He always replied:	No, it is impossible, the contract was awarded to Pierre Boucher, the lowest tenderer, and nothing can be changed. Finally, I find a letter written by the hon. member for Dorchester who, I suppose, has developed a certain fondness for the county of Kamouraska since he contributed with his excellent friend the Solicitor General to the splendid victory I won in 1925. The hon. member for Dorchester, since it is signed O. Gagnon, said:

Dear Mr. Anderson,
re Riviere Ouelle Mail.
In view of the fact that M. Lebel is carrying the mail between the central post office anid the two small ipost offices which will be closed. I think it is only fair that Lebel gets the contract.
Yours truly,
O. Gagnon.
And then, instructions were given and I can find absolutely nothing in this file that justifies this change of front on the part of the minister. Here we have the man who put in the lowest tender; his contract is signed, and there is only a letter signed O. Gagnon which the hon. minister can possibly identify more readily than I could, and that results in the department facing about in this manner. And they fall back on that because the gentleman who holds the contract says he made a mistake which he is very slow in pointing out and stating that he is prepared to correct that mistake by submitting a tender at a price lower by $5 than the tender price of the man who had secured the contract.

I wish to say
to the hon. member for Kamouraska that I will ask the superintendent, Mr. Anderson, to give me all possible information on the matter and I will pass this information on to him.

I am anxious not to delay the passing of the estimates of the Postmaster General; it is now almost six o'clock, and if there are no other hon. members to speak I will be as brief as possible in order to put through these estimates by six o'clock. I have waited all afternoon; I did not want to take the place of any other hon. gentleman, so I hope the committee will bear with me in the few remarks I have to make. As I sat listening this afternoon I was reminded of scenes that occurred in this house in 1929; to-day I saw the chickens come home to roost. I did not feel so sorry for the Postmaster General as I did for some of his colleagues, who had to listen to complaints with regard to violations of the regulations, and complaints with regard to the way dismissals have been made. These same complaints were made against me in 1928, when I was Postmaster General.
With those opening remarks I wish to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to a case in which I think action should be taken immediately, not in the interests of the officials concerned but in the interests of the principle laid down in the Civil Service Act with regard to the method of making appointments. I have in my hand the record with regard to a vacancy at Oliver Siding in the

Supply-Post Office
county of Restigouche. I am not going into the question of the dismissal or the appointment, but the report of the district superintendent at St. John should have been forwarded long ago to the Post Office Department. In that report I find these words:
... it may very reasonably prove in the interests of the department eventually if the appointment of a permanent postmaster be delayed for as long a period as possible. The rating has been signed with this qualification.
I want to direct the attention of the PostMaster General to this condition of affairs. No superintendent should be allowed to make a report like this. The reason for this recommendation is that the man who was then temporarily in charge of the office, after a dismissal had been made for political reasons- and this office comes under the Civil Service Commission-was under a cloud for some sort of misdemeanor, and bitter complaints had been sent to the department. This man was brought before the courts on a criminal charge, but the grand jury threw it out, I do not say whether or not this man was guilty of wrongdoing; I know nothing of the case, but I say a report of this kind should not be sent in, recommending that this man be not appointed permanently for the present and that the qualifications be not sent to the Civil Service Commission until it is seen whether or not the man will prove worthy of the confidence that was placed in him in the beginning. That is a practice that should be stopped, and the district superintendent who countenanced that report should be reprimanded. Nothing like this should be allowed to prevail in any department of the government. If a man is worthy of being appointed to a position it should be given him; he should not be appointed temporarily in order to see if his reputation will improve. I may add that in this case a couple of returned soldiers wrote the district superintendent at St. John for forms with which to apply for that position, but they were never favoured with a reply.
There is another case to which I should like to refer, having to do with the appointment of a postmaster at St. Quentin, in the county of Restigouche. I do not want the minister to inquire into the qualifications of that man but I do want him to inquire into his nationality. My information is that he is an American subject, and if he is not a British subject he has no right to a position under the Civil Service Commission.
Then there is a case in Green Point, in my own county, to which I should like to refer.
A Madame Thomas Fournier was appointed temporarily to this vacancy. I want to remind the Postmaster General that under the act a married woman cannot be appointed postmistress if her husband is capable of supporting the family. In addition to that, some ten or twelve years ago, when members of this family looked after the post office at Green Point, they were dismissed because of shortages in their accounts, and I should like that matter to be taken into serious consideration. I believe there is a scheme on foot to have some of the people who were connected with those dismissed for shortages appointed in charge of that office.
I have one other case to draw to the attention of the minister, and I hope to conclude in a few minutes. This is a case in the county of Colchester, Nova Scotia. If the minister does not know it already I want to inform him of the way in which some of his superintendents are notifying postmasters to get off the job. I have here a letter dated Halifax, March 29, 1932, addressed to Mr. A. J. Yuill, Old Barns, Nova Scotia, reading as follows:
Dear Sir:
I have received instructions from the department at Ottawa to relieve you of the post office and to transfer it temporarily to Mr. Harold Crowe Chisholm. The reasons for the change are that the proposed site is more suitable and centrally located. You will be advised of the date on which the transfer is to take place.
That is signed by the district superintendent; the man is dismissed and then held in office until the transfer takes place. If I had been that postmaster I would have walked out the moment I received that notice. The reason given is that the other place is more centrally located. Well, the old post office is situated, we will say, where the Postmaster General is sitting, and the new one is situated where I am standing in relation to him. It is only 60 feet across the street; they are opposite each other. Why that reason was given, therefore, that it was more centrally located, I do not know.
The Postmaster General said last night that during the time I had the honour to be Postmaster General I had made 317 dismissals without investigation, without report, or without reason. He must have been wrongly informed by somebody. I know that he would not do me an injustice. However, I have here the record which I have submitted to the house at different times in regard to dismissals, and that record I will place on Hansard once more. From October, 1926, to
Supply-Post Office

April, 1928, there were 473 dismissals made by myself, and during that time 383 of these dismissals were made on report submitted either by inspectors or by investigating commissioners. That is on record. Among those there were 56 dismissed for shortages, abandonment of office, arrest of postmasters. There were 47 due to unsatisfactory management, and on investigation and report. There were 49 due to changes in site, on the report of inspectors, and there were 4 reinstatements. In interest of service, on report, there were 91, and no reason given, 90. The next list shows 84. All of these 84 were dismissed on certain reports after investigation, except 2. In the next list there are 45, and of these, in every case except 2, there were reports from inspectors or investigating commissioners. This list is made up as follows:	Shortages,
abandonment of office, and arrests, 22; unsatisfactory management, on reports of inspectors, 9; changing site contrary to orders, 1; interest of service, on report, 2; changes in site, on report, 6; and political partisanship, 5.
That makes a total of 602 up to the beginning of the year 1930. I have not the record with me from that date up to June, 1930, but up to the present time, under my hon. friend opposite, there have been 597 dismissals in eighteen months, or an average of 33 per month, whereas during my time there were 602 dismissals in a period of four years, or about forty-dive or forty-six months-I am not counting the 400 referred to by the hon. member for Temiseouata-and that gives an average of 14 a month. So that we have 14 a month on my part as compared with 33 on the part of the present minister.
I should like to have gone into some other matters such as postage stamps, for example. I see that there have been laid on the table supplementary estimates in which an additional amount of $266,000 is asked for. I understand that this is for extra cost of postage stamps and other matters connected with the department. As I say, I should like to have been able to deal with these matters, but I wish to facilitate, as far as I can, the passing of these estimates, and with these few remarks that I have made I will now do what I can to help the minister get the estimates through.

speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I should like to say a word.
Certainly.

As I look at this book
of estimates, I see two pages in front of me and I see that in nearly every case the effort that has been made to decrease the estimates has been followed by success. The increases

are ini the Department of National Revenue, and they are considerable in amount. These increases, however, are more apparent than real, having been occasioned by the treatment which the board of customs has received. The result of the appropriations that are laid before the committee to-night in connection with National Revenue is that there is a decrease of over $3,140,000. I was very anxious to say that and I am pleased the hon. member for North Waterloo gave me the opportunity, because the. initial page was spoiled by these large increases for which, as a department, we are not responsible at this time. They are a bookkeeping entry, if I may so put it, taken into the account for the first time, and hereafter these items will appear under National Revenue, civil government.
I presume the amount of increase, then, will mean a decrease in the other very large item, No. 277?
My hon. friend is right.

It is a transfer from one to the other. In connection with the board of customs, does my hon. friend really think the 100 or more employees who are supposed to be under the control of that board are so in effect? I used to think it was pretty much of a misnomer; perhaps my hon. friend does not see it in that way.
I would agree with my hon. friend. The answer to his question is no.

Perhaps my hon. friend desires to make a statement explaining the decreases in this item.

If my hon. friend will permit me, I do not know that I am very anxious to talk, but since I have been invited and drawn to my feet, let me make this brief statement. When these estimates were prepared I was impressed, with the absolute necessity of special economy. I knew we had to cut according to the cloth; I felt that the cloth was scanty and I still feel that is so. When these estimates were first prepared I thought it might be possible to cut them even to the very quick, with the result that the estimates of this department are put in at a figure that does not allow us efficiently to carry on. I realize, as I am sure all hon. members do, that if a business needs money, the expenditure of it may mean either the saving of the business or a large profit to it. I was forced to the conclusion, after these estimates were prepared, as they were a couple of months ago, that we needed more money,
Supply-National Revenue

I believe I might almost congratulate the minister on the fact that he has been able so substantially to reduce his estimates. The only point which occurs to me is the one which he has mentioned himself.
That I have gone too far?

Yes, perhaps. After all the Department of National Revenue is successful only to the degree to which it collects revenues. That collection takes the greatest degree of supervision and vigilance and cannot be accomplished without certain activities. For instance there must be adequate allowance for salaries and travelling expenses of officers of the inspection, investigation and andit services. The investigation and audit services are particularly important because it is through the exercise of those services that the department is able to ascertain where the revenues are not being paid as they should be. I am wondering whether the minister has gone too far, and that through the elimination of certain expenditures he may lose more than he gains. That is, he may lose 
more through loss of revenue than he gains by the cut. I merely make that observation in passing. If he is not, it might be fair to assume that the late government spent too much-an accusation 1 should not like to admit. There is no doubt the cut is very large. In the first item there is a decrease of almost 12,000,000. I presume that is partially attributable to the fact that there has been a ten per cent reduction in civil servants' salaries. I should like to ask the minister, however, whether he is quite certain that he is retaining a sufficient auditing and investigating staff to get the necessary results by way of revenue, and I am wondering if he is not losing revenue because of the decrease in his expenditures.

The interrogation of the hon. member is most appropriate, and the subject to which he has directed my attention is the one which has troubled me most. Finally, however, after going into executive sessions with the officers of the department we have decided that if the supplementary vote is granted we can carry through with a strong arm. That being so, in these times I am not going to fight for any margin to work upon, because we need all the margins we can get to carry on the business of the country. As my hon. friend has said, the whole thing amounts to only a straight business proposition. Will the sum for which we ask advance the interests of the country, or will it not? After the best consideration we in the department have been able to give, we have come to the conclusion that the sum before the committee is sufficient.
I Shall now show how the $1,964,860 is made up. The estimate for the year 1932-33 is $6,600,000, as compared with $8,564,860 for the year 1931-32, or a decrease of $1,964,860. This sum is made up as follows:
Vacancies not provided for, 330; attached to that, $568,245; ten per cent on salaries, $657,661; decrease in contingencies, $738,954; amount required in 1932-33, $6,925,000; amount approved in estimate, $6,600,000.
Hon. members will note that the amount short is $325,000, which is made up in the supplementary estimates.

So that we may form a better judgment could the minister tell me how many peopl.e were employed in the audit and investigation branches, and how many are now employed in those branches. In other words, what is the reduction in personnel?

The number on the inspection branch, the investigation and values branch, the investigation and drawbacks branch and the audit branch totals 277. Their

Supply-National Revenue
salaries amount to $738,4*,-less ten per cent, of course. I do not like to advertise this fact too freely, but I must say that the vacancies have not been filled. Where there was a chance of sailing along with the smaller staff, and yet making the same time, these vacancies have not been filled. Therefore the number is less to-day by reason of our manipulation of the vacancies.
Have any been laid off?
No.

I see in connection with the preventive service there is an item of $1,340,000. Last year it was $2,108,991, or a reduction of $768,991. I suppose that reduction is due to the fact that the service has been taken over by the mounted police. No doubt the answer to that query, at least to some extent, would be "Yes." There is still left however a very large sum for the preventive service.
I am not suggesting it is too much, but I should like to know where the dividing line comes between the estimate for the preventive service which now goes to the mounted police branch of the service, and that which still continues within the control of the department itself. I gathered from statements made about two weeks ago that the preventive service is now taken over by the mounted police. Is this vote for the branch of the mounted police doing preventive work, or is it for the Department of National Revenue? Where is the dividing line?

My answer is this: These estimates were prepared before the mounted police finally took over the preventive service. The result is that the mounted police have all those who were formerly in the preventive service with the exception of fifty-eight men and seventy who have retired from the service. This item, if adopted, will be turned over to the mounted police except what is necessary to provide for the fifty-eight men whom we must retain. They are retained, I may say, because they are investigators, examiners and auditors. The mounted police, we hope, will detect crime, and we will follow it up.

Now we know that in the
mounted police force the salaries are lower than they were in the preventive service. Was the estimate made on the basis of the old salaries or of the salaries paid to the mounted police?
It was made in anticipation of the cut.

So in future this estimate
for the preventive service will almost entirely disappear from the estimates of the Department of National Revenue?
That is right.

Last year I recall half a
million dollars was added to the usual estimate for the administration of the Income War Tax Act.

I was under the impression
that it was about half a million dollars. I asked at the time the then Minister of Finance -the Prime Minister-why the amount was increased, and he stated I thought \ er>
fairly-that he felt by the expenditure of the additional sum so much more income tax would be collected that the outlay would be well repaid. I see this year the amount s reduced. Would not the same argument apply this year as applied last?

We hope to do what
we did last year. We spent the money out of the income tax vote. As I am informed none of this $350,000 was infringed upon, but owing to the extra money we found available in the vote and spent we added a good many thousand dollars to the revenue. We propose to keep on in the same way, if we can.

I desire to ask the
minister a question, but frankly I cannot find any particular vote of his that covers it. There is in a sense hanging over certain of our industries something in the way of a threat of prohibitory tariff legislation now before the United States Congress, dealing with coal, oil, lumber and copper. I am particularly interested in lumber; I am not very familiar with the other commodities. We have a favourable trade balance in lumber with the United States, notwithstanding that we import a veiy substantial quantity of American lumber. But balancing our imports of the lumber industry as an industry against our exports, my opinion is that the balance is in favour of that country because of rhe fact that there is being used in the lumber industry in all parts of Canada, particularly in British Columbia and to a considerable degree in Ontario, a very large volume of equipment in the way of logging, saw mill and planing mill machinery imported from the United States. But without going into details, the lumber industry itself estimates that 'the importation of this American equipment more than offsets our favourable trade
Supply-National Revenue

balance in lumber with the United States. In the eastern provinces we are suffering to a very considerable degree by the dumping of lumber products of certain grades, mainly into Ontario and Quebec. Under existing legislation has the Department of National Revenue power to protect the lumber industry against this dumping if the proposed tariff is put into effect at Washington? In other words, if the United States authorities determine to make it impossible for us to trade with them at all in lumber, can we, without new legislation being passed, protect our lumber industry? If the minister could give me that information the whole lumber trade would appreciate it very much.

As I think members of the committee pretty well know, if there is any attack made which, in the language of section 43, "prejudicially or injuriously affects the interests of Canadian producers" a special value for duty can be fixed on instructions from the governor in council to the Minister of National Revenue. If unfair or slaughter trade is introduced into Canada by the United States, there is a ready weapon at hand in that section of our law. It was placed upon the statute books at the instance of a Liberal government in regard to natural products, and therein in my opinion they did well. It has been carried somewhat further by legislation which this parliament enacted covering any products which were dumped or slaughtered here to the prejudice of those engaged in the business of those products in this country. My answer therefore would be yes.
Thank you very much.

With regard to duties affecting lumber coming from the United States, is it not true that last June this government put on a special duty of one per cent, and the American government immediately retaliated, in fact practically put a gun to the head of my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue and told him that if he did not take off his duty they would put a special duty of II per thousand feet on boards, planks and deals of fir, pine, spruce, hemlock or larch in the rough or not further manufactured than dressed on one side when imported from Canada, with the result that my hon. friend as Minister of National Revenue had to go to the governor in council and ask for an order taking back what this government has done?
My hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) is right in his basic facts.
Thanks, very much.
He is wrong in centering that matter around me.
You are the head of the Department of National Revenue.

I had nothing whatever to do with putting on the one per cent excise tax. It seems that at the present time there is in the United States tariff something that some of us were not altogether too familiar with. It involved only one per cent, and we cloaked that one per cent by describing it as an excise tax. There is in the United States tariff a provision, speaking from memory, that if any tax is placed against United States lumber a tax of SI per thousand, or some such figure, comes into effect as a countervailing tariff, so when our one per cent excise tax was passed they came back with this provision. What was the reasonable thing to do? We replied that we did not want the $1 a thousand against us, and it was not applied against Canadian lumber because we took off the one per cent tax here. I am sure my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough will not blame me for advocating the removal of that tax.

My hon. friend knows that I
believe in free trade. I do not believe in any tariffs, any restrictions or any regulations which will affect the trade of Canada. But if I understood correctly what my hon. friend said in reply to the hon. member for East Algoma, the minister was not quite frank. Consequently I take him to task, because if my information is correct this special tax against American lumber was passed by this government on June 2, and our United States friends immediately protested.
I know my hon. friend does not want to misinterpret what was done. This was not a special tax against United States lumber; it was a one per cent excise tax on everything.

It was not a tax applied by the Liberal government, so I consider it an extra, special tax. In any case the fact remains that this tax was put on by the present government, and immediately that was done the United States government said to us, through our representative at Washington, "If you do not take off this tax we will put a duty of $1 per thousand against all lumber and manufactured wood products coming from your country." If my information is correct the United States government went even further and said to our representative, "We are not satisfied that you should say you will take off the tax," though hon. gentlemen opposite

Supply-National Revenue
were glad to do so; the United States government said, "We want you to pass an order in council." A few years ago, when we were in power and hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting on this side of the house, we were told that our tariff policy was made in Washington. Here, however, is a distinct case where this government, not at the request but at the insistence of the United States, passed an order in council removing the one per cent excise tax on lumber and leaving it on all the other goods imported into this country.

Was the order in council
framed in Washington?

I would not be surprised, although I have no definite information. I do know that the United States were not satisfied until the order in council passed by this government was placed in the hands of their government, to show good faith. At the insistence of the United States this government was compelled to remove this special duty on lumber, and I should like to know why that was done in the case of lumber, at the request of the United States, when it was not done in connection with all other products.
Carried.
No, I want an answer.
You will not get it.

I have a few questions to
ask, which I think the minister can answer very easily. Some two years ago we made provision for the introduction of the eight hour day in connection with the employees of the department. That was not completed at the time I left the department, and I should like to know if it now has full application.

There is an order in
council dealing with the Department of National Revenue, which is copper lined and iron bound with regard to the eight hour day. I wondered why some other departments were not affected at the same time. That order in council is being lived up to, though it has cost the department an immense amount of money. I have been told that by reason of the eight hour day something like $600,000 of extra expense has been put upon the department. That was the figure mentioned to me; it is not accurate at present, but I know I am safe in saying, from what has come before me, that a very large sum of money has had to be expended in order to carry out that provision. I do not wish to be understood as complaining, but my hon. friend from North Waterloo knows how
necessary it is to have men at the ports at all times, and as a result the expense has been very considerable. I think the answer to my hon. friend's question, however, is that it is being lived up to in letter and in spirit.

Just a word with regard to the sales tax. Some two years ago large sums of money were owing the department by brewers and distillers. I am not now referring to those cases which were taken to the courts. Other firms owed large sums of money, and it was necessary to nurse them along a bit. I should like to ask the minister if those amounts have been collected or the indebtedness materially reduced.
The amounts have been materially reduced, and I think I have helped reduce them.

Were any applications for
licences made last year?
There was one application, but if my memory serves me aright no licence was issued.

Is the department still
observing the practice of consulting with the provinces with regard to the issuing of licences?
Yes.

In connection with amounts owed by brewers and distillers, there is one other question. The department took legal action against several brewers and distillers with regard to the export of liquor or beer; in many cases a settlement was made voluntarily and they agreed to pay, usually in instalments. Then I understand that one case, the Carling case, was carried to the privy council, where a decision -was rendered against the department. Have any of the other concerns, who perhaps had cases more or less similar to the Carling case, applied for the refund of the amounts paid, and if so, what is the attitude of the department in this connection?

As my hon. friend knows, the Carling case was won by the department in each court until the privy council was reached. The privy council, however, held that the department was wrong. Before the case reached the privy council, as my hon. friend has said, settlements were made with indivdual brewers. Naturally, after the judgment of the privy council, some of those concerns who had paid their taxes thought that if they had continued in litigation a little longer they might have enjoyed the fine result
Supply-National Revenue

that came to the Carling company. But the settlement with these brewers was made before the judgment of the privy council. The settlements were made upon the advice of their attorneys, acting for them in these suits, and, may I say, they were made independently of what the privy council judgment might be in the Carling case. They are being held to these settlements, and not one has received any consideration by trying to hark back to the position they would have been in if they had travelled along with the Carling people all through.

One other question in connection with liquor matters. In view of the prohibition of export to the United States via Canadian ports and the consequent export of liquor to the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, from which points we do not know where the liquor went, although we may have a suspicion, and in view of the fact that the exporters of liquor and beer had paid no excise tax, may I ask whether there is reason to believe that any of that liquor was smuggled back into Canada? Is there any suspicion that this has taken place, and if so, to what extent?

I do not think my hon. friend should ask me what my suspicions are, but since I have been in the office I have certainly learned more about smuggling than I knew before, and if I may venture a guess, I should say that some of it has returned. How much, I do not know.
Has it been necessary to increase the preventive service in consequence?
No, but that amendment to the Export Act meant a serious falling-off in the revenue.

The excise tax having been increased from one to three per cent, what is the position of the Department of National Revenue with respect to the order in council passed on October 20, 1931, revoking the excise tax so far as the importation of lumber from the United States was concerned? Is lumber from the United States now free of the excise tax of three per cent or not?

I think that would be a proper question for the Minister of Finance. I see that I have not made myself clear to at least one member of the committee in regard to lumber. The position of lumber was this. There was in the United States tariff a couiftervailing provision that if any

duty, even the slightest, were put on-and they took note of one per cent-then, if I remember rightly, they put on a rate of SI a thousand.
One dollar and fifty cents.

Whatever the figure is, the argument is the same. That figure went on. It was not fair, since the balance of trade was largely in our favour, that for the sake of one per cent excise tax we should deny to those who shipped lumber from Canada the privilege of doing so, because they would be met with a prohibitive tariff. If anyone objects to our action in that regard, then he will have to have his argument with somebody else.
But there are other items of trade besides lumber in which we have a favourable balance with the United States.

Yes, but there is no
countervailing item in the United States tariff.
Yes, there is.
Not many.

There are several in connection with which there is a balance of trade in favour of Canada. Why should lumber be picked out in this regard? If it is a fair proposition to take the excise tax off lumber, surely it is just as fair and in the interests of the common people of the country that the excise tax should be taken off other commodities. I asked the minister whether the order in council passed on October 20 last, taking off the one per cent tax on lumber, would apply to the increase from one to three per cent brought down by the Minister of Finance in his budget, and he sidestepped my question by referring me to his colleague. I have in my hand a copy of the order in council which was passed, and the name of the Minister of Finance is not mentioned in it. It was the Minister of National Revenue who applied to the governor in council for the passing of the order in council.
It certainly was.

Then why not take the responsibility? Why should the minister want to burden the Minister of Finance any further? Goodness knows he has enough trouble now without the hon. gentleman trying to place this additional burden on him. The order in council states that His Excellency the Governor General in Council "on the recommendation of the Minister of National Revenue", and so on. Not the Prime Minister, who was

Supply-National Revenue
Minister of Finance at that time, nor the present Minister of Finance, but the Minister of National Revenue. It was on his recommendation that it was done. Why, then, when I ask a fair and reasonable question, should the minister practically tell me that I ought not to ask it on his estimates but wait until the estimates of the Minister of Finance come down? I contend that if it is fair to take the excise tax off lumber imported into Canada, other industries which suffer by having imposed upon them this tax of three per cent should be treated in the same way. The discrimination is not fair. All industries in Canada, whether they be farming, fishing, lumbering, or mining, should be treated alike. No special favour should be shown any one industry, and if the Minister of National Revenue is going to recommend to the government the taking off of the excise tax in connection with lumber, it is only right that every other industry should be placed in the same position.

There is nothing in the
Minister of National Revenue having made the recommendation to council. As is well known, all recommendations in connection with the administration of revenue are supposed to be made to council by the Minister of National Revenue. That's that. With regard to sidestepping the hon. gentleman's question, I was not aware that I was doing anything of the kind. The hon. gentleman is no more apt to sidestep than I am; I do not think either of us is given to that. The point, however, is that there was in the United States tariff a special countervailing item, and it was felt that in the balance the lumber industry of the country would be benefited if that one per cent, as it was then-there was no question of three per cent at that time- were not insisted upon. The moment the proposition was put before one, it was yielded to as the only proper thing to be done. My hon. friend from Bruce says that it is $1.50 a thousand. Would it not then be a fine thing to have imposed on us $1.50 a thousand for the sake of one per cent? Even the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough would not suggest that.
Hear, hear.

If he can suggest any other item that travels parallel with lumber and in regard to which the United States tariff has a countervailing duty, and if such an item has not received consideration, I think I can say on behalf of the government 41701-200
that it will. But I do not think any other item exists. An hon. gentleman speaks of coal, but we have not trodden on the toes of the coal industry. There have been threats to do it but it has not been done.
Twenty-five cents.

The minister has hardly given the information asked for by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). I think it is clear that the one per cent excise tax imposed on imports by the Minister of Finance was treated by the American government as a duty.
That is right.

The Prime Minister distinctly told us that this was not a duty. However, it is a tax on American imports and the American government has treated it as a duty. Because of the one per cent so-called excise tax imposed by Canada on American lumber importations, the American government availed themselves of the countervailing duty provision in their customs act and applied a duty of SI .50 per thousand feet on Canadian lumber shipped into the United States. The minister was very wise in passing the order in council on October 20 of last year under the provisions of which lumber coming in from the United States was exempted from the payment of the one per cent excise tax. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough wants to know what is going to be done with the three per cent excise tax put on this year. There is no order in council governing the 3 per cent tax and there is no doubt the $1.50 countervailing duty will now apply against Canadian lumber entering the United States. Is the minister going to change the order in council to exempt American lumber from the three per cent excise tax? Every hon. member knows how the lumber industry in this country has suffered during the last few years. Every hon. member knows that the American market is one of the few profitable markets left to our lumbermen. Every hon. member knows that the lumbering industry is in a very bad way and if we lose the American market or have to pay $1.50 per thousand feet in duty it will mean more unemployment, and, goodness knows, unemployment is bad enough at the present time. I think either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue should give a clear statement to the committee as to whether or not this three per cent excise tax shall apply to lumber, then the lumbermen will know how to act.

The three per cent is in the same position as the one per cent; it will not apply.

I respectfully submit
that the order in council of October 20 does not cover the situation to-day; it cancels the one per cent tax on lumber. Is the minister going to amend the order in council to make it exempt from the three per cent tax?
The higher tax does not apply.

I beg the minister's pardon. The order in council distinctly states that the one per cent excise tax as incorporated in last year's budget shall not apply to American lumber; that order in council does not cover this year's budget.

My hon. friend asked that question, I think, last year, and I believe the answer given at that time was that no separate record was kept. Duties are being paid every business day and we do not label them as dumping duties, we take them all in as part of our receipts.

I am not desirous of putting the minister or the department to any more trouble than is necessary, but I do not see how they can keep their records straight without having this information. I have under my hand bulletin No. 3185, dated January 30, 1932, refined granulaited sugar, fixing the value of refined granulated sugar at $2.30 per 100 pounds. Would the minister mind telling us who asked for this order in council, and how this value of $2.30 was reached?
It was asked for by the sugar beet farmers and by the sugar beet refining industry located at Wallaeeburg and Chatham.

There is an understanding, is there not, that wherever such a request is made, those making it must satisfy the minister that they are in a position to supply the demand. When this order in council was passed, were the sugar beet farmers and refiners in a position to satisfy the market for sugar?
It was understood that this would be for the benefit of the market. There were 6,000 sugar beet farmers who depended upon this order in council.
This was in January. I do not think the beets were grown then. Had those farmers grown enough beets to be in a position to satisfy the market?
The contracts are made in January. It would be the beets harvested in the fall of the year.

Had they on hand enough
beets, grown the previous year, to satisfy the market until the next crop came along?

I do not know that they had a supply of beets on hand, but we were looking forward. This legislation in my view, supported as I was by counsel, was proper; ad from whom information could be got were in favour of this being done and it was done.
Then my hon. friend had this order in council passed in January in order immediately to shut out sugar which would be replaced next fall by sugar from beets to be grown this summer; is that the idea?
The idea is that otherwise no beets would have been sown this spring, no crop of sugar beets would have been raised and 6,000 farmers for whom my hon. friend has often shown sympathy-
I never asked for protection for them.

*-and in wnom he has a keen interest would not have grown beets so that two industries would have suffered.

I love the Canadian dollar, but I like any other money I can get. I apply the same principle to the people of this country.

That is very good logic, but I can remember last year members of the government expressing indignation that the people of the United States did not value our dollar as highly as we did. Yes, it increased the price of

I say that not only 6,000 beet sugar growers, but 16,000 potato growing farmers were affected by the policy of the Minister of National Revenue with regard to the dumping duty he placed on sugar.
Then, another class of people in addition to the farmers was affected. I have heard the expression that fish and potatoes go together. Because of the mistaken policy of this government, by carrying out the policy enunciated a moment ago by the minister, not only did it affect the farmers of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick but it affected the great fishing industry of the maritime provinces. Cuba offers one of our principal fish markets, and my information is-I think I know what I am talking about-that the minute my hon. friend and his government introduced this special legislation and had it so arranged that he could put any value he liked on sugar, the sugar growers in Cuba, or the government of Cuba, deliberately and properly, increased or doubled the duty on fish and potatoes going into that country. Ruined?

I should like to revert to the matter of lumber, and the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for East Algoma. Probably I did not hear the minister correctly, but the answer seemed to satisfy the hon. member. Whether his satisfaction was due to understanding it or due to some congenital or hereditary respect for the minister as a member of his party, I do not know. The complaint of the hon. member for East Algoma was that the people to the south of us, in a bill now before congress, were imposing a heavy and almost prohibitive duty on our lumber going into the United States. He also mentioned coal. I think it is now ascertained, however, that there is a provision in connection with coal which entirely relieves us in Canada of any danger from that source. The hon. member said that the bill would prove very dangerous to our lumber trade, and in that I heartily agree. I did not know it was a question of moment in the east, but it certainly is worthy of very serious consideration in British Columbia. The duty would very materially affect the lumber trade, which, as my hon. friend sitting beside me says, is now in a very bad condition

The hon. member for East Algoma stated the case, and as I understood it he asked the minister to take some action. He did not however definitely state what action he thought should be taken. If I heard the minister's reply correctly I think he quoted section 42 of the Customs Act.
Section 43.

And he said if any lumber or anything else entered Canada in a manner prejudicial to the manufacturer or producer of that article in Canada, he would be quite pleased to put on the dumping duty. In all courtesy I submit that is hardly an answer; it is not a solution of the difficulty. The grievance is that the United States are threatening to exclude our lumber, and I cannot quite understand how by preventing their lumber from coming in we are meeting the situation. Probably the lumber in connection with which the minister expresses his willingness to put on the dumping duty might not be coming in in a manner prejudicial to the producer. If it had 'been, the duty would have been put on already.
As a rule lumber does not come in and go out at the same points. We find our lumber entering the United States from British Columbia; large quantities in the shape of hard wood or other lumber not readily available in Canada come into the eastern provinces from the United States. The remedy as I see it is not the putting on of an illogical or possibly improper dumping duty. Instead of going in for retaliation some other action should be taken. Tariff wars in the past have not been successful anywhere, and I am wondering if we could not adopt some measure of reciprocity, if I may use the word. I think the word used on the continent of Europe, when they do not wish a strict definition, is "conversations." The word does not bind anyone to anything until some progress has been made. I would suggest that our ambassador at Washington should be instructed to enter into "conversations" with the powers that be with a view to arranging some measure of reciprocity in regard to lumber. He should suggest that it is desirable that we be allowed to ship our lumber from British Columbia into the United States. It is badly needed in the north western states where the farmers are in difficulties. Their only lumber supply comes from British Columbia. On the other hand American hardwood lumber is needed and could be shipped into our eastern provinces. By such action probably more could be accomplished than by waving the bloody shirt and talking about excessive dumping
duties. In case I have misunderstood the minister, would he amplify the policy he proposes to meet the situation? This is a very urgent matter, so far as the lumber business of British Columbia is concerned.

I do not think the
situation has been made clear, but I shall attempt to say what was in my mind when I answered the hon. member for East Algoma. I understood from his remarks that there was a danger of the United States putting on a heavy duty against our Canadian lumber. I think that is the understanding of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. If that is done, the countervailing arrangement, if we may so describe it, is gone. Then if they put the duty on our lumber entering the United States, and at the same time dump their lumber here to spoil our markets-
Not necessarily.
That is how it was put by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson).

Pardon me. He said they
would not let our lumber go in. He said nothing of their lumber coming in to prejudice our market.

Yes, he sp-oke of our
market being prejudiced by their action.

I was not present when the member for Antigonish-Guysborough first brought this matter to the attention of the minister, but from what I have been told I think he explained it so that members of the committee are familiar with the facts. The point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is that this order in council which was passed repealing section 88 Of the Special War Revenue Act, chapter 54, was ultra vires. The order in council states that:
The governor in council on the recommendation of the minister acting under the powers conferred upon him by section 11 of the customs tariff as amended is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered that certain lumber shall be exempt from payment of the tax of one per cent.
That is to say, by order in council he repealed a statute passed by this parliament. Reference is made to section 11 of the customs tariff. I think members of the committee will remember that when this excise tax was being discussed last year my hon. friend from Wey-bum (Mr. Young) brought up the question that it was a customs tax. This was indignantly denied on the other side; they said it was an excise tax. Nevertheless in order
Supply-National Revenue

to get authority to repeal that section they refer to customs tariff section 11. I challenge my hon. friend the minister, who is a 'lawyer, to assert that this section gives him any authority. The section provides:
The governor in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on goods-
Not excise tax.
-imported into Canada from any other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for reductions on Canadian products granted by any such country or countries.
There was no .reduction from the United States.
Oh yes, there was.

No, the United States simply said: If you put a tax of one per cent on our lumber going into Canada, there is automatically under our tariff act a countervailing duty of SI.50 a thousand on Canadian lumber.
Hear, hear.

They said: If you dare tax our lumber we will put into effect the $1.50 duty. There it is. I will read it to the minister:
Boards, planks and deals of fir, pine, spruce, hemlock or larch, in the rough or not further manufactured than planed or dressed on one side, when imported from a country contiguous to the continental United States, which country admits free of duty similar lumber from the United States, shall be exempted from the duty of $1 per thousand feet.
Is it a $1 or $1.50?
Maybe I have the old one.
It is $1.

I do not remember. But the moment we imposed that excise tax, automatically the United States government was obliged to impose their tariff. Now, forsooth, we say:	We will repeal this act
by repealing the excise tax on the ground that we get a reduction from the other country. We did not get a reduction; the other country imposed something on us and we had to repeal our duty. That is the first authority the minister had to rely on.
What about the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act?

He was not quite sure and he endeavours to combine two authorities entirely separate. In effect he says:	One
act does not go far enough, but if we can cite seventeen sections of seventeen different acts we may be able to put them together

and get them right. I will come to the second authority which my hon. friend relied on. I think it will be admitted that the first is no good, but it cannot be any better when combined with the second one. The second authority relied on is section 91 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. And do you know, Mr. Chairman, what it speaks of? Remission of duties. The minister must know what "remission" is. It certainly is not repeal of a statute. The section reads:
1.	The governor in council, whenever he deems it right and conducive to the public good, may remit any duty or toll payable to His Majesty, imposed or authorized to be imposed by any act of the parliament of Canada, or by any act or ordinance of the legislature of the late province of Canada, or of any of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, British Columbia or Prince Edward Island, in force in Canada, and relating to any matter within the scope of the powers of the parliament thereof, or any forfeiture or pecuniary penalty imposed or authorized to be imposed by any such act or ordinance for any contravention of the laws relating to the collection of the revenue, or to the management of any public work producing toll or revenue, although any part of such forfeiture or penalty is given by law to the informer,-
And so on.
2.	Such remission may be total or partial, conditional or unconditional, and may be granted either before or after, or pending any suit-
And so on.
3.	If the remission is conditional, the condition, if accepted by the person to whom the remission is accorded,-
That is, by the United States.
-shall be lawful and valid, and the performance thereof, or the remission only, if unconditional shall have the same effect as if the remission had been made after the duty, toll, penalty or forfeiture had been sued for and recovered
And so on.
4.	No remission shall be made in any case-
In any case.
-unless such case has been considered, and the remission, whether total or partial, conditional or unconditional, has been recommended by the treasury board, and sanctioned and ordered by the governor in council.
I submit this section deals entirely with the remission of duty which has been collected, and does not deal with the repeal of a section of an act passed by this parliament. It cannot by any interpretation be made to read that the governor in council has the right to say that the tax imposed on a certain class of commodities shall be repealed. Remission implies the refunding of a toll which has already been paid. The very word "remit"

Supply-National Revenue
means to give back. The action taken by the government is simply tantamount to saying: This law shall not apply to lumber coming in from the United States.
That is all.

There is the situation. I
contend that these orders in council were beyond the powers of the governor in council, that this excise tax is still in force, and that if the Minister of Finance persists in making a three per cent tax instead of a one per cent tax, even if the government is right in its contention, that the one per cent tax is repealed, certainly there will still be two per cent payable on every bit of lumber that comes in from the United States. '
That is the point.

The only honest, straightforward, decent way to do this business is for the minister when he brings down his special war tax legislation to write into it that lumber shall be one of the articles exempted from the payment of that tax. That is the only way to do it, because if he does it in any other way I submit he will be doing the wrong thing, he will be introducing legislation which is slipshod, and which, I firmly believe, will not stand a test before any court in Canada. As my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) paints out to me, the order in council reads:
His Excellency the Governor General in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of National Revenue and under the powers conferred by section 11 of the customs tariff,-
Which I submit does not apply.
-as amended by chapter 30 of the statutes of 1931, and by section 91 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act,

Which I submit only applies to remissions.
*-and any other powers thereto enabling.
So they said .to themselves, "We will take one section of one act and perhaps we will get somewhere, and if that is not strong enough we will take another act and perhaps we will get somewhere with it. We have not time to look uip all the statutes; we are very busy men, working twenty-four or forty-eight hours a day. We will just include any other powers we have, and if we do not have them we will say so anyway and a lot of people will believe it." I wish to protest against that sort of legislation; I sincerely hope a minister of procedure will be appointed by the government so that these things may be done regularly.

I have another protest to register. My hon. friend from Weyburn asked the minister what was the basis on which the minimum value for duty of refined granulated sugar was fixed at $2.30 per hundred pounds, and the minister said he did not know. Then my hon. friend from Weyburn asked what was the machinery, how it was arrived at, and whether there was any investigation, and the minister replied that the officers of the department fixed that point. My hon. friend from Weyburn persisted and asked on what basis it was fixed, but the minister replied, "You will have to ask them." Have we come to that, Mr. Chairman? Is that parliamentary government? The tariff is .changed, not by parliament, and when we ask the reasons for the change we are told we will have to ask the officers of a certain department. That is no longer parliamentary government; that is bureaucratic government with a vengeance. Last year the government insisted on enacting a law .creating a tariff board; that was the main legislation of last session. This body was constituted for the purpose of investigating all matters concerning changes in the tariff; they were to study and consider all applications which might .be made. More than one year has elapsed since this law was passed but still we have no .tariff board. We are to have an Imperial conference this summer at which tariff matters will be discussed with all the other nations of .the empire, but no board' has been appointed to investigate these matters. Surely if there was need for a tariff board that need exists at the present time.
I do protest against the answer of my hon. friend that we should apply to the officers of the department in order to learn why the value of $2.30 was fixed. Surely hon, members of this house have the right to know what tariff changes are made, when they are made by order in council and on what basis they have been made, without being obliged to inquire of the officers of the department.

First I might reply to my hon. friend from Quebec South, who has left the chamber. His statement seemed rather peculiar; he assumed that because the United States called this one per cent tax a customs duty, and contended that it thus came within their law, it was essentially a customs tax. Then my hon. friend proceeded to say that the customs tariff cannot be read to apply, so he denies his own argument. I do not think it is necessary to proceed further except to say that hon. members of this house who belong
Supply-National Revenue

to the privy council will know that order after order is drawn up making remissions or refunds under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
Does the minister accept the interpretation of the United States?
I do not think it matters. What is the difference between an excise tax and an excise duty?
Why call a customs duty an excise duty?

Because we like that name, and its application is different from the application of a customs duty. This excise tax was intended to cover everything; it applied to lumber, but when it became important to take it off lumber it was removed. This tax was treated in a different way from our customs duties, which of course are regulated by the customs tariff. But I am not going to split hairs with anyone who says it should be called a customs duty, because certainly it is collected at our ports when the goods come in.
Now I should like to say a word in reply to my hon. friend from Quebec East. It almost makes me smile to think what would have happened if the tariff board created last session had been functioning in the interval. The tariff board was not appointed because with the kaleidoscopic world changes that have been taking place this has not been a proper time for the operation of such a board. Look at the authority given that board; what were its duties? The board was to investigate the cost of raw material, the costs of manufacture, labour conditions and so on, and gather such information as the Minister of Finance might request. What would have happened if this board had been operating on September 21 last? Everything they might have done under that authority would have been practically worthless, but this legislation which we have placed on the statute books has been made use of. This was not for the tariff board; it was for the governor in council, working with the Minister of .National Revenue, under express enactment. My hon. friends opposite had no objection to that when they were in power; as I say, it was initiated by them and they made use of it time and time again. I am sure every ex-minister knows that, so surely no objection can be taken now. My hon. friend from Quebec East became quite fervent in saying that the governor in council had acted without the advice of the tariff board, but my hon. friend knows that even if there had been a tariff 
board it would not have been part of the functions of that board to look after this matter.
My hon. friend made another statement which is hardly correct, and I think perhaps I can see why it was made. I did not say that the basis of this calculation on refined granulated sugar was made only by the department. First we had our investigators go into the matter and then, in consultation with members of council, we asked the officers of the department to figure out what the basis should be. I cannot do the arithmetic, and I think my hon. friend will be fair enough not to ask me to do it at this time. As I told him, I know that the freight rates from the south and the freight rates from Montreal to Toronto entered into the computation. A demonstration was made, which assisted in coming to a conclusion. As I say, I cannot go through the arithmetic, though I know the facts, but it was decided by the governor in council, after investigation, that this was a proper thing to do, so it was done. I hardly think my hon. friend is fair when he imagines-
Who made the investigation?

The investigation was
made chiefly by Mr. Breadner and Mr. Richards, officers of the department. Mr. McGregor, representing the sugar refiners, was also consulted.
Cane or beet refiners?
Both.

I may say-

I thought the hon. gentleman
had concluded.

I may say to the hon.

I want to say to the hon.
gentleman that there is one section of Canada that appreciates the fact that there is in power to-day a government with backbone and determination enough to put into effect policies that are in the interests of the producers of Canada. The hon. member has asked what effect this policy has had. Let me tell him this. I pleaded with the former Minister of National Revenue to put into force dumping duties against the huge importations from the United States, but they would do nothing. For five years I pleaded with the government which the hon. gentleman supported, to take some steps to stop these considerable importations, but they did absolutely nothing. At that time, when our cabbages were ready in western Ontario, the Canadian market was flooded with Virginia cabbages; when our potatoes were ready, we found the Canadian market flooded with Michigan potatoes; when our tomatoes were ready, Mississippi tomatoes came in and flooded the market; when our cucumbers were ready, Louisiana cucumbers were coming in in vast quantities. The hon. gentleman wishes to know what this government did, and what the effect of its policy has been. On April 22, 1931, the government passed an order in council putting a market value of 15 cents per pound on asparagus, and I may tell the hon. member for Lisgar that this had the effect of protecting the producers of Canadian asparagus. A little later on, on June 11, they put on a rate of 4 cents against American cabbage, and that permitted the growers of cabbage in Canada to sell their product on the Canadian market. That is what it did, Mr. Member for Lisgar. On June 11, an order in council was passed imposing 8 cents a pound on carrots, and I could go all down the line, mentioning the various orders in council that have been passed, every one of them in the interests of the producers in the district I have the honour to represent. Let me say to the hon. gentleman that I have the honour to represent in this house the most diversifield farming section in Canada, and the growers of South Essex appreciate the action of the government in 1931, and the action which they propose to take in 1932, to protect Canadian growers and give them the Canadian market, which otherwise would be flooded with American produce.
And now will the hon. gentleman answer the other part of my question and say how the revenue has been affected.
I will say this to the hon. member, that any country that is built up on imports is bound to fail.
I am glad that I have some friends who can come to my help-
I was only expressing the sentiments of the growers of South Essex.

I may say to the hon. member for Lisgar that complaints have not come to us in any number at all. The growers are satisfied with what has been done, and they are anxious to have what was done last year repeated this year. My hon. friends opposite must have believed in the policy themselves, because they did the same thing. As regards the revenue, it has fallen off; but let the hon. gentleman remember that the revenues of this country compare very favourably with those of other countries. Naturally there has been less business and therefore less revenue, but I do not think this country is suffering very much when the business of buying and selling, which is natural to the country, is done within the country. If, therefore, a little loss in customs revenue has meant work to Canadians in Canada, and business in this country, I, for one, am satisfied to see that diminution in revenue. Just one more observation in this connection. I do not see why these questions with respect to policy should be addressed to me. I am willing to answer if I am called upon to do so, but I am trying to administer the department, and if there is any question with regard to administration, such as the question in relation to lumber, then I think it is quite proper that I should be asked to say something by way of explanation or in support of what we have done; and if there is any condemnation, very well. But that it should be left to this late date in the session for me to deal with policies of government-that, I submit, is not expected from the Minister of National Revenue. However, I shall be glad, if it will satisfy hon. members, to continue in my humble way to try to answer any questions that may be asked.
I do not think the minister can evade responsibility for answering as to the effects of his own policy.
If the hon. member will permit me, I did answer.
Perhaps I misunderstood the minister, but I understood him to say that he should not be expected to answer-

I asked the question for this reason. We all remember that the usual argument that was advanced against the importation of fruit and vegetables from other countries was that by the time the Canadian

fruits and vegetables were ready for the market the edge had been taken off people's appetites and that they had been satisfied. We remember how the Minister of Railways used to go up and down the country declaiming against the many million dollars' worth of fruits and vegetables that were coming in from abroad. I believe the figure he used to quote was $40,000,000. Of course we all know that this included all kinds of fruit and vegetables that were never grown in Canada at all. apiece. The minister says:	No, you shall
not bring them in. A friend of mine who wished to secure a maid to help his wife in the house, believed he could get one in the dried out districts of Saskatchewan.

Oh, oh.
