gentlemen to laugh, but if they were in that position, they would not laugh. That was the situation. While people in this country are going in rags, in their bare feet, the minister boasts in the house that he has deprived them of the opportunity to secure dresses at thirty-three and a third cents apiece.

I am not going to delay the passing of this estimate, but I should like to make one observation, particularly because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has come into the chamber. The hon. member for East Algoma referred to a probable duty on lumber being put into effect by the United States and referred also to the disastrous result this action might have on the Canadian lumber industry. Later on the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough discussed with the minister the fact that the countervailing duty of $1.50 per 1,000 feet applied on Canadian lumber by virtue of the fact that we had applied a one per cent excise duty on United States lumber entering Canada. The hon. member for East Algoma, when he was speaking of the possible duty being applied by the United States, appealed to the Minister of National Revenue and, I think, to his colleagues in the government, that if this were done, it would be advisable to retaliate against the United States by imposing a duty on their lumber entering Canada. I do not suppose I shall have another opportunity this session, so I now want to warn the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government that there could be no more foolish or destructive policy for the government of Canada to adopt than to retaliate by placing a duty on lumber entering Canada from the United States.
All lumber unfortunately has been treated in our customs tariff under one item. Lumber consists of the production of a variety of trees and has many uses. We in Canada are quite

Supply-National Revenue
dependent, whether we like it or not, on the United States for oak lumber, hickory lumber and walnut lumber. The hon. member for Lincoln knows- quite well that hickory lumber is essential in the manufacture of certain commodities in which he is interested; I know that walnut lumber is essential in the manufacture of certain commodities in which I am interested, and I warn the minister not to treat this item of lumber as though it were just one commodity. The lumber item should be divided into several classes; then we could treat it properly with regard to the question of customs duties. I appeal to the minister and the government, should the United States impose a duty against Canadian lumber, not to jeopardize and injure the existing industry in Canada by retaliating and putting a duty against raw material which it simply must secure from the United States if we are to keep our men employed in certain branches of the woodworking industry. What the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said is quite true; the proper thing to do is to conduct negotiations with the United States with a view to keeping lumber duty free between the two countries. Canada gets the best of the lumber trade between the two countries; we ship to the United States more than we buy from them, and what lumber we buy is of a type we do not grow. I advise the minister not to indulge in any foolish policy of tariff reprisals on lumber even if the government has the power to do so.

I should like to know
the regulations in respect of the entry of books of an educational character published in Great Britain but not published in this country. The reason I ask the question is this: to-day I received a letter from a friend of mine in my riding, who, while a farmer and not a very wealthy one, is by way of being a student of economics. From time to time he orders publications from the old country and this one, when it reached Red Deer, which is a customs port, was held there for duty purposes. Believing that such books were admitted free, he protested to the collector there who informed him that the only books of an educational character exempt from duty were books not printed or reprinted in Canada which were actually included in the curricula of Canadian universities, schools or colleges, and that this book, of which my friend unfortunately neglected to give me the name, but which I am sure from my knowledge of him, was educational, was not in any curriculum. It was published by George Allen and Unwin of London, England. It was apparently on economics. He stated that he was not particularly concerned with the small amount of duty that he was obliged to pay on this book, but he was concerned as to the policy, because he thought-and in this I very strongly agree with him-that brains, ideas, should come in as far as possible duty free. If they are desirable books used in the study of economies or any other branch of education, I think they should be allowed to come in without payment of duty. As I do not know the book in question I cannot argue about it, therefore I am asking the minister the practice in regard to books of an educational character printed and published in the old country, but not in this country. I refer to books not found upon the curricula of Canadian universities, schools or colleges; because the minister realizes that there a.re many works of an educational character, but modem in tendency, which have not found their places upon the shelves of our schools. I hope the time may come, however, when they will.

Cadet services-to meet balance of commitments, $260,000.

Why is this item introduced in the supplementaries when we were encouraged by the main estimates tc think there was a reduction?
Supply-National Defence

I am guilty. My
intention was to try to get along with the former amount. I was unaware at the time that this vote is for the school year beginning the first of September last and ending in June. So we are committed for the whole amount now.

It is not really an
addition?

Oh, no. The hon.
member will recall it was $400,000 last year; it is $40,000 less with this supplementary.
What does the minister propose doing next year,-leaving it as it is now?

In all probability
we will keep on about the same. It may be necessary to cut down to a certain extent, but in a general way we want to keep the movement going.

I protest against this expenditure. As the committee knows, some of us have been opposed to the cadet movement. We do not think it is a good thing to encourage the military spirit on the part of boys, as we believe this movement does. But at this particular time, when civil servants are being cut ten per cent, when large numbers of men are being laid off, when the unemployed are having a desperate time even to exist, and when a man died in Montreal the other day of poisoning from food taken from the dump, which is just one more example of the desperate straits to which men are reduced, it seems to me absurd that we should have in the supplementary estimates $260,000 more for cadet training in schools. Some of us have protested previously that we do not believe the Dominion government has any right to go into the educational field in this way; that it is a distinct invasion of provincial rights. I am aware that the provinces have consented to this arrangement. I am glad to think that in my own city, after much effort, we have managed to keep cadet training out of our public schools. We intend to keep on doing so, but in other places the officers do everything in their power to induce school boards to take it up. Quite often the boards are reluctant to do so, and many parents are strongly opposed to having their children receive cadet training, but it is done on the urgent solicitation of officers of the Department of National Defence.
We have brought up these points before, but I wish to do so again. In these particular circumstances and with the conditions that prevail to-day there seems no justification

whatever for placing this amount in the supplementary estimates and keeping the vote where it was in previous years. In any case, if the arrangements are such that the minister is in honour bound to carry them forward this year, it seems to me that at least he should give the assurance to the house that there will be cuts as soon as this school year is over.

May I suggest to the
minister that in these times of hardship this money might be used to buy shoes and clothing for the children of the unemployed who because of their lack of clothing are unable to attend school. I know that in many cities and towns in different parts of the country there are children who cannot go to school because they are not properly clothed, so I suggest that instead of encouraging this drumbeating we permit children to attend school with proper clothing. I am glad to support the timely suggestions of the hon. member for Southeast Grey and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If the minister is unable to accept them, could he not give this money to institutions that are supported by private charity? There is such an institution in Montreal called La Maison Ignace Bourget, which was founded by a member of the press gallery and some of his friends to care for old men in that city. At present they are sheltering, feeding and clothing about three hundred people. It is an admirable work, and I believe we should give all we possibly can to the poor in order to help them through these hard times.

I have said so often what I think about this cadet training that there is no need to go into it at any great length to-night. But I want to state once more that it is educationally unsound, because instead of developing a child it uses the child for an objective quite outside the child itself. I notice we have a new, outstanding authority for that view; I refer to Doctor A. S. Lamb, head of the McGill school of physical education, who has stated it many times, with much force, both in the press and on the public platform. For that reason I am against cadet training. My own belief is that if the instructors were not paid so much per head we would not hear very much about cadet training. I have come to the conclusion that boys do not like it; they prefer something that is joyous and free and that means something to themselves. It may be that on parade, when everything is shined up, they like the show, just as most people do, but I think boys rather hate cadet training day by day. They are not interested in it, and if it were not for the department urging them on the one side and the teachers urging them on

Supply-National Defence
the other-the department because it is trying to keep a military machine in some sort of readiness, and the teachers because they make money out of it-I do not think we would hear anything about cadets. It should not be carried on, no matter how well we could afford it, because it is bad from every point of view; but this year we cannot afford it. It is simply ridiculous to spend money in order to have small boys strutting up and down a yard with guns when other children, as hon. members have truly said, have not clothes to wear or food to eat to enable them to go to school.
To-day I had in my office a man of mature years, though still young, who six months ago completed a two year term in one of our penitentiaries. He came out with a determination to do the right thing, and he has made a great effort. During the six months he has been out he has kept himself strictly honest; he has not done anything he feared he might do. He has kept away from the old crowd ;*he has sought work and up to the present he has been able to keep himself, but now he is in desperate straits. He asked for a job, a job of any kind; he was only too willing to work, and he is just one man out of hundreds. We have scores of men lying all over our parks, some of them hardly more than boys. They are desperate and they will fill our criminal institutions if something is not done about it. We should use every cent we can get together to save those who can be saved instead of spending money on this sort of nonsense, though I am not sure that this is any worse than the yearly drill we are to have. I see we are going on with the nonpermanent active milita this year. It is a terrible waste of money, and there is no justification for it under present conditions.
There is just one other point to which I should like to refer. Even from the military side, cadet training is useless. It does not make soldiers; it is simply a waste of money. If that amount of money were spent on real physical education, teaching the boys to play the game, as seems to have been so successful in English public schools, it would mean a great deal. I think we found during the great war that it took as long to train cadets as it took to train those who had never been cadets. From every point of view I protest against this vote. I was glad to hear the minister say, however, that this is not an actual increase, that the money has been practically spent already. It should be cut out altogether. I am wondering if we must go on forever training boys in military tactics just because Strathcona created a fund. It
would have been better if he had taken it with him, if we must keep on forever doing this sort of thing. I do not like to think that because a trust was established years ago we must go on spending money in this way year after year. We will go on forever if we do not find some way of stopping it. We do need physical education. There is a great movement in that direction in our schools and universities, but that is quite a different thing from military drill.
I should like to ask the minister to let this item stand in order that my hon. friend from St. Johns-Iberville may speak to it.

Personally, I think there

Mr. LaVERGNE: I hope the vote will not be reduced, because, so far as Quebec is concerned, we have more cadets in that province than anywhere else in Canada, and this is a splendid educational movement. It forms the mind of the child, gives him an idea of discipline, and teaches him how to carry himself and how to answer his superiors. I am glad to say that so far as we are concerned the cadet movement is progressing year by year and doing great good to the children of the province, physically, mentally and morally.

I am strongly against that kind of discipline-
Mr. LaVERGNE: And my hon. friend is the best example of what he says.

Give me a chance to
speak; you are not in the chair. I have the floor and it is my turn now. My hon. friend,
[Mr. Sutherland.)
I believe, is a colonel in the army, but I want to tell him we are not his soldiers. I am a friend of his, but I do not depend on him. Here we are all free, and the Prime Minister, when he sits in his place, is only the first among equals, as I have already said. We are all the same. That is why I take this opportunity to speak as a free lance. As regards that word "discipline," may I say that if I had been in Ottawa I should probably have attended the dinner given in honour of the Minister of Railways. I should likely have done so because I like him personally; I would have attended a dinner given, not to the Minister of Railways, but to a very fine man. And if I had been there and had heard the Prime Minister complimenting the hon. gentleman on his spirit of discipline, I would have protested, because that is no compliment to a member of the House of Commons. As I say, we are all free and must continue to exercise our freedom. I am in favour of gymnastics, because it is good for children; it helps them to grow up into healthy men and women. I believe in gymnastics on the old principle of mens sana in eorpore sano; but I am strongly against instilling militaristic ideas into the miinds of children. No doubt we must have respect for order, but there is a great difference between a proper understanding of order in the state and the militaristic idea of discipline. Although I am a free lance I am strongly in favour of social order; I believe in it just as firmly as my hon. friend from Montmagny does; but I am not at all strong for the idea of having children carry guns when they are only ten years of age. It is good for them to do their daily dozen, and children should go in for healthful sports, and it is a good deal cheaper, if you are to spend money on physical training for children, to buy them footballs and baseballs and things of that kind than to buy a lot of prizes and fancy uniforms and guns and trumpets and so on. Let the government buy them footballs and bats and baseballs. Let them go in for sports which will help to make them healthy. That will be just as good for them as this cadet training.
If I take up the time of the committee now it is only because I have been prevented before from doing so. And when a "man, whoever he may be, says that a member of the House of Commons is retarding progress because he expresses his views, let me say to my hon. friend that I am here as a free man. I have never been a cadet in my life, and that is why I express myself freely in a free House of Commons in a free country. We must have absolute freedom. Had I been

brought up a cadet, perhaps I should not now say what I am saying, for fear of being unpleasant to someone. But as a free man, I speak freely. That is all I have to say at present.

We have been told

This year we have seen a good deal in the press about three youths who were expelled from the Windsor Technical School because they would not take cadet training. If that is not compulsion, I should be happy to have the minister explain what it is.

I am very much in

In view of the general circumstances now existing throughout the country does the minister not think he is hurting himself, his cause and his government by continuing to vote this amount of money? There is not a man or woman in the country acquainted with the actual conditions but who would praise the minister if he eliminated this vote during the present economic depression. It is quite true that it is not a great amount but it looks pretty big to the unemployed and to those who are trying to serve the unemployed and steady them during this time of stress. The voting of $360,000 for the drilling of little boys in schools is not the thing to do during times like these. I am opposed to this vote in both good and bad times, but in view of the present economic conditions I think it should be eliminated.

Of course the hon.
gentleman must realize that there are two sides to this question. Many people throughout Canada have a different idea from his. These grants are not being forced on the school boards; if they do not want them they do not have to take them. Since the main estimates were brought down I have had many representations from people all over the country protesting against the reduction. This is not a military organization; the physical training is what justifies it. The dis-

cipline entailed, is a most excellent thing for young people at a time like this. Discipline and physical training are the very essence of the cadet corps, not militarism.

Perhaps it

No.

Oh, no.

Was it an
underestimate?
Yes, an underestimate on my part.

In view of the fact that some $84,000 is for salaries of personnel and the rest for travelling expenses, and so on, I am not surprised that at a time like this the drill instructors, lecturers and military gentlemen do not want to be deprived of their little perquisites. I should have been surprised had the minister not received protests, but I am surprised at his unwillingness to tell these people that in times like this when children are starving they should be willing to forego their perquisites. I attended a public school in the old country where we were given excellent physical training by a sergeant-major of the British regular army, but he did not train us with guns, he used Swedish drills. He trained us in a gymnasium properly equipped with the necessary apparatus to build up such health and strength as our physical structure would permit. We did not have this silly gun drilling, this standing at arms, this saluting the sergeant-major and all the rest of that rot against which resentment is developing at the present time. The minister is not helping his cause or his government by bringing forward this vote this year.

I rise again to protest against this vote. I realize, as does the minister, that physical training and discipline are of great value to children, but there are other tilings of more value at a time like this. First things should come first. We realize this when we visit districts, as I have during the past winter, and find little villages with their three and four roomed schools closed and the children fiorced to run on the streets. It is very hard to go back to those people and justify a vote like this being granted to schools for (physical training when .other children cannot get the first principles of education.

When the primary schools in certain districts are being closed, it is difficult for one to justify a vote of $260,000 for cadet training. If you could have the schools open and have this cadet course going on as well, that would be all right, but these are strenuous times and we are in a period of depression, so that I think we might well curtail some of these activities.

The minister says he is

They have cut out some $200,000 in provincial grants which were being used in an endeavour to eliminate certain social diseases. They have eliminated a small grant of $20,000 to the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, an organization that has done invaluable work throughout Canada in helping to keep our people healthy. Salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol and fisheries protection services, $1,022,000.

This item, Mr. Chairman, is as good as any to permit me to refer the Minister of Fisheries to the discussion that he and I have had during the last two weeks, particularly with regard to the lobster season in the western end of Nova Scotia. Possibly the committee will remember that last winter from December first to January fifteenth a special lobster fishing season was granted to the fishermen at the western end of Nova Scotia instead of unemployment relief. Hon. members can hardly realize what it means to be pulling lobster traps in open boats in December and January weather. Some of them fished from Seal island, eighteen miles out in the Atlantic ocean, and hon. members can imagine what that involved during that inclement season of the year. But in return for that concession they were penalized; their regular season which runs from March first to May thirty-first was cut by fifteen days.
I objected to it at the time on the groimd that it was not fair to make those men pay for their own unemployment relief. It simply meant they were being given an opportunity to get enough food for themselves and families, but this relief was charged back to them by cutting off two weeks from their spring season. They got something like eleven thousand hundredweight of lobsters, probably one-fourth or one-fifth of the regular catch, and owing to the stormy weather they lost quite a bit of their gear. Then in March they had to fit out again. It was probably one of the worst March months in many years, and several of the men hardly took a lobster during that month. Representations began to be made to me early in April for the restoration of the season to the end of May. These I forwarded to the minister, and he gave them consideration, but he advised me that nothing could be done until the first of May, by which time the returns would come in showing what kind of season the fishermen had had. The return disclosed that counting the winter season and the two months up to May first, they had caught something like
24,000	or 25,000 hundredweight, when the normal oatch would be from 40,000 to 50,000 hundredweight or perhaps more. It was represented to the minister that these men had had a very hard time, having lost a great deal of their gear, and were just beginning to pay expenses when they had to cease fishing. Finally after a good deal of
Supply-Fisheries

discussion the minister extended the season until May twentieth; putting it the other way, he took only ten days off the spring season instead of fifteen as he planned when he gave the men their relief season last December. The minister objected to restoring the full season further, stating that representations had come to him that the price would go down if the request of the men were granted. Now I am informed that the lobster fishing is just really beginning, and if these men had ten days more during which to fish they would be able to make perhaps between $100 and $200 as a result of their total lobster fishing season. At the present time they hope they may be able to pay expenses up to May 20; that is all. I am told that the price has gone up five cents in the last three or four days of the season, just at the time when the minister was advised that the price would go down if the men were allowed to fish. I submit that these fishermen have not been given a fair deal. I know the minister has considered the matter carefully and that representations have been made to him by fishermen in the eastern section of the province against extending the season. But I contend that these men in western Nova Scotia were entitled to their own season, that they were not asking any special consideration. On behalf of the fishermen of the western section of Nova Scotia I protest most strongly against the way in which this matter has been handled. There has been talk about preserving the lobster fisheries, and that we would lose all our lobsters if these men were allowed to fish. As I told the minister the other night, I have a newspaper clipping in my office which indicates that away back in 1895 it was predicted that there would be no more lobsters around Cape Sable island, yet they have been fishing lobsters there ever since. The lobster crop has been up and down, and the theories that have been advanced about the depletion of the lobster have not been borne out. These men should be given a chance to live, and the regulations should be relaxed for their benefit. Again I protest as vigorously as 1 know how against the treatment of these men. The department has given all the other fishermen their full season, but these men have been cut off simply because of the fact that they had a relief season in December.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am sorry the faon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough is not in his seat, so that I might call on him to answer my hon. friend. He is aware that

all the members from the eastern and northern parts of the province are strongly opposed to the extension of the season from the fifteenth to the end of May. As he has just said, the usual lobster fishing season in the western end of Nova Scotia runs from March first to the thirty-first of May. Last fall on account of a petition for a fall fishing season, we decided to authorize this from December first to January fifteenth, and as an offset close fishing this spring on May fifteenth instead of the end of the month. Unfortunately March, as stated by my hon. friend, was so stormy that a very small catch was made. The April catch has been reasonably good. We received petitions from the eastern and northern fishing areas asking us not to extend the season from the fifteenth to the end of May. According to our figures the catch this year has been as good as if not better than in previous years.

I know the minister wants to be fair, and I am sure he will acknowledge that the catch has been fair only if you count the catch taken in the special relief season. The catch in the regular season was only about half the normal catch.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That is so, but they had their catches during December and January, and there were many reasons why the season should not be extended for too long a period. In dealing with this matter we must take into consideration two things. One is the effect an extension of the season will have on, the future of the fisheries. My hon. friend knows very well that we have to protect the fisheries and that is why, when the winter season is extended to include December and January, the spring season cannot be extended also. I am told that in 1921 the season in western Nova Scotia was extended, with the result that the fisheries were so badly depleted that conditions did not become reasonably normal until 1925. These are the facts.
The other question to be considered is the effect an extension will have on the other areas. The western area ships all its lobsters nine inches or more in length to United States markets. The live lobster business is the most paying branch of the industry on the different parts of the coast where it is carried on. In southeastern Nova Scotia the season this year opened on the 16th, and in the whole gulf of St. Lawrence division and down through the straits of Canso, to and including the most of Richmond county, the season opened about a week later. Each of these districts ships large quantities Of live lobsters to Boston, as my hon. friend knows, and the

Supply-Fisheries
market conditions there are so bad that, with large supplies coming, the prices are likely to fall to such an extent that the fishermen will not make anything. We had requests some time ago for the extension of the season to May 31, but at the same time we had representations from Boston dealers and from the eastern and northern parts of the fisheries to the effect that prices in Boston would fall if this were done. In March, when western Nova Scotia was the only area shipping and the catches were very light, prices in Boston were from $40 to $50 per crate. Last week, when my hon. friend came to my office, with fairly large shipments going in from both eastern and western Nova Scotia, the price fell to $19, which does not make it a very paying proposition, and it was felt that the price would fall as low as $15. The Boston dealers are all counselling against an extension, as they say that because of economic conditions the market this year cannot absorb large quantities of lobsters. We are told that if these are shipped the prices are bound to fall to very low levels. One of the largest shippers of the gulf division who is now in Boston wired about two weeks ago saying it would be wholly unfair to the gulf division to extend the season in western Nova Scotia.
These facts are well known to my hon. friend, but even though everyone in northern and eastern sections protested we extended the season by about five days. I understood that every one was satisfied; we received no protests following that extension. Of course there was some protest from the eastern fishermen, but I understood that the western people were satisfied. I know my hon. friend is pleading the case of the fishermen of his constituency, but we must take into consideration also the interests of other parts of eastern Canada.

fishing season. You can take that as axiomatic. So when I was approached with the request that this winter season be extended, let me say that one of the arguments they used in support of the request was that it would assist in the relief of unemployment, though that was by no means their strongest point. They wanted to share during a longer period of the year in the profitable Boston market. Having had the experience of which I have spoken, I said I would consider their request upon one condition, and that was that they should consent to a shortening of the summer season. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not propose to be put through a catechism as to whether it was John Jones or William Smith, but I do say that I took pains to send Mr. Cowie to that section of the country, and he conferred with groups of fishermen and with those who were identified with the industry to a sufficient extent to get a proper expression of opinion representative of the views of the fishermen in the areas concernnd. They agreed that they would not ask for an extension.
I say I was at pains to have that course taken, because I knew very well that if they secured this extra six weeks during the winter season they would come along this summer and ask for an extension covering the same weeks as have obtained hitherto. Now, if you please, whatever the reason may be, here they are, and I am not finding fault with my hon. friend for pleading the cause of the fishermen. They want to have their cake and eat it. I say that the acting minister is to be commended, because of the special conditions obtaining, for extending the season for five days, but in doing that I think he went as far as he could be expected to go in the circumstances. We must remember that we must have regard for the interests of the fishermen not only in this particular area but throughout the whole of the maritime prov-
Supply-Fisheries

inces. All these men are shipping to the one market, and the seasons must be rotated so the advantage will be divided equally among the lobster fishermen along the various parts of the shore.
I hope my hon. friend the acting minister will forgive me for having taken up this time, but because of the knowledge I had of the incident I thought I should advise my hon. friend who I am sure wants the whole story.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is moved that the committee rise and report progress.
I am in the hands of the committee, but surely I might say a word first.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We promised to rise at
a reasonable time. The shorthand staff of this house is a little weary, and I had intended to move that the committee rise at 11.45. I think perhaps under the circumstances the hon. gentleman will realize that we cannot, finish this item to-night, and in view of the work that has been done by the shorthand staff I think the committee had better rise.
I could finish in three minutes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But could the item be
finished?

I want to say to my
hon. friend the former Minister of Fisheries that I do not know who was seen by his representative down there. I only know this, that the representations came to me very directly that there had been no agreement of any kind with regard to the six weeks' season, and I do not think that my hon. friend should really talk about an agreement under circumstances of this kind. The circumstances were these. The men needed something to see them through the winter, for they had had a very much more difficult time than usual. My hon. friend knows that the price of ground fish was very low and the market poor. These men had to have unemployment relief, and the government simply said to them, "You can go out and fish lobsters." They were allowed to go out and fish for six weeks, and now the minister says that there was a bargain whereby these men, under these conditions, were going to be precluded from asking, not for an extension, but merely for the regular season. Both the minister and the ex-minister have used the term extension. No one suggests an extension. The ex-minister declares that it had frequently been the practice of these men to request an extension, but I point.out to him that this year all they are asking for is the 
regular season. I submit, therefore, that my hon. friend cannot talk about an agreement..
In the second place, with regard to the other people affected, may 1 ask how it is that this year my hon. friends happen to be so particular about the other people who are affected when every other year the season has been the same and there has been no suggestion of cutting ten days off the season in western Nova Scotia in order to accommodate someone else either on the north shore or in the east. This year ten days are cut off because, we are told, somebody else is going to be injured. As I said to the minister the other night, are you going to cut off ten days merely because someone else does not like the season? Of course the competitors in other sections would like to see the season shortened as much as possible. But the point is that the seasons are prescribed by order in council and have been for some time, and they do overlap. Now the packers and the Boston dealers saw their chance this year and they said, "We are not going to have an overlapping season. Ten days are cut off the fellows in western Nova Scotia and we will see to it that these ten days are kept off." That is not much of an argument, that someone else in some other part of the province wanted to see these men continue to be deprived of the ten days.
Thirdly, with regard to conservation. The Minister of Finance and I do not know a great deal about lobsters, although we were both born near the gulf shore. But I want to say to him-I think he will agree with me-that the lobster fishery has been going on there for a long time and it has taken more than ten days' fishing to destroy the industry. I think that all this solicitude about the conservation of lobsters down there at this particular time could well be left to the fishermen themselves, to the people who, after all, have to make their living out of the business. I do not think that we need be so anxious to do for them what they can do far better for themselves.
As to the price, the minister has not answered what I have said. According to a letter I have received from a director of the Maritime Fisheries Federation, the price has gone up-not down-five cents per pound in the last five days. That is in the face of all the representations which my hon. friend had from the Boston dealers, and I say to him again that the Boston dealers had better be left out of it and the fishermen given a chance for their lives, particularly at this time. I make this representation because letters have come to me with regjard to the matter. If the minister has not yet received any com-

Montreal Harbour Commission
plaint, he will get my letter in the morning. One point more; I ask my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Fisheries: suppose there had been an agreement, even if there had been a signed bond that they would not ask for their regular season, what has he to say about the situation when we find the month of March practically a total blank? I have two letters, both written on March 29. I quote an extract from the first:
Times are hard; the lobstermen have not been able to even set their traps yet, owing to the gales which have prevailed here since the first of March.
From the second letter I quote the following:
The men here have only a few traps out, and as it is awful rough to-day, would imagine that very few of the traps will be left.
I submit, therefore, that the men were justified in asking that the minister maintain the season for the ten days. Questions of conservation, price and other people's views do not enter into the situation where not only the rights but the very living of the lobster-men of western Nova Scotia are concerned.
Progress reported.
